utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Professor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We will continue now with re-examination by Mr. Zecevic. Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Professor.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, in the course of yesterday, my esteemed colleague Mr. Hannis suggested that when you discussed those changes to the constitution of Serbia and the amendments of 1989 and the constitution of 1990, he suggested that Albanians were opposed to amending the constitution of 1989 and later the constitution of 1990 because it deprived them of the rights they had under the constitution of 1974. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Albanians did not lose any rights; they had all the rights as a national minority. It is the province as a political and territorial entity that was set up in the constitution on a different plain.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, for the duration of the 1974 constitution where the autonomous province had all those rights that it had under the 1974 constitution, did Albanians make any outcries even then?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In 1981, for instance, there was a major outcry, although under that constitution, as you said yourself, Albanians had the greatest possible level of autonomy. But they were never happy with just autonomy. They have always wanted an independent state of Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So in 1981 when that constitution was in force and when they had all those rights that you called unique, even in theory, a unique case that an autonomous province should have all those rights and authority, they were not happy even then. Do you remember that the slogan: "Kosovo as a republic," appeared then for the first time?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in that insurgence of 1981 their slogan was: "Kosovo as a republic." They envisaged that Kosovo should become a federal unit at first, but when they realised that was impossible they started calling for secession from the Federation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That insurgence of 1981 was suppressed, if I can put it that way, in an operation of the joint forces of the police of the entire SFRY?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's the federal Ministry of Interior that reacted --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not sure how this arises out of my cross-examination. I don't remember talking about 1981.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think it arises from your suggestion that the amendments of the constitution in 1990 were at the root of the unrest and the suggestion is -- or at least the evidence that the witness is giving is that the unrest is much more deep-seated. I have difficulty at the moment knowing who this evidence favours most, but I do think it arises out of cross-examination. So please continue, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, do you remember the question?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, I do. At that time, it was the federal secretariat because we didn't have ministries then. It was the federal secretariat of the interior, that is, an organ of the Federation intervened to suppress that insurgence in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. Yesterday on page 13541, line 23, there was discussion about how the delegation or members of the delegation of Serbia in Rambouillet acted less than seriously. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If I remember well, in the course of your examination-in-chief you said - and I believe you repeated it yesterday - the names of our experts who worked there, including Professor Kutlesic and yourself?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we were part of the delegation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You said at one point, I believe, that on one occasion with American negotiators Jim O'Brien, and the name of the other eludes me for the moment.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Levitsky, John Levitsky.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You said you worked with them on one occasion from early evening to the small hours, the American expert team and our delegation worked together?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We were sitting at a desk, and on that same podium but slightly further away, Mr. Wolfgang Petritsch sat all that time, from early evening until dawn of the next day.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Again yesterday on page 13556, lines 14 through 16, Mr. Hannis asked you about that alleged comment of Mr. Milutinovic, about that massacre, something like in the case of bombing there will be a massacre on Kosovo. You said, of course, that you hadn't heard that but that you were not together with Mr. Milutinovic all the time. That's what you said in response to Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Milutinovic had his freedom of movement and I was restricted to that castle.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, according to Mr. Petritsch, that comment was made one night during the discussions between Mr. Milutinovic on one hand and Mr. Mayorski and Mr. Petritsch on the other hand, and allegedly it was then that Mr. Milutinovic made this comment. That happened inside the castle. Did anybody out of that troika ever or maybe one of their associates or did Mayorski tell you perhaps, What is this that the president of Serbia is saying? Did anybody ever had any comments in your hearing on this statement?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, on the contrary. I read in books about Rambouillet that Mr. Petritsch had said that that statement had been made by Mr. Stambuk. I can't remember the exact book and the author, but I believe it was the book of Miodrag Mitic entitled: "How Rambouillet Happened to Us." I believe I read there that this comment was made by Mr. Stambuk.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. On page 13568, lines 16 through 24, you discussed with Mr. Hannis the meeting that took place during the war with late Dr. Ibrahim Rugova, you recall that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: My learned friend suggested that Mr. Rugova and Mr. Merovci were under house arrest or something like that. You attended those talks from the very beginning until the very end, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Did Mr. Rugova or maybe Mr. Merovci ever mention in the course of those talks that they were under house arrest, that they had a problem, or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never. I first heard that from the Prosecutor when he examined me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Would you think it would have stood to reason that they should inform you and Mr. Milutinovic if they had a problem because you had come from Belgrade, you were not part of that situation in Pristina?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would have been normal. It would have been only expected of them to voice the complaints they had, if any, but it was a very cordial meeting and Mr. Rugova even made a gift to Mr. Milutinovic on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 13578, lines, or rather, the next page as well, you discussed the debate made by Mr. Milutinovic at the Assembly session, you recall that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You were there in Rambouillet, in Paris as head of the delegation. You made your report to the Assembly of Serbia, and after several speakers had their turn, Mr. Milutinovic stood up. You heard his speech, his expose. Would you say that Mr. Milutinovic deceived the Assembly in any way by saying something that was not true, that was not consistent with the facts?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour, that calls for speculation and that was not a point that I was arguing in cross-examination, I don't believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is this not something we can read for ourselves and that you can make submissions about, Mr. Zecevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I do, Your Honour -- I understand Your Honours, but it was -- the allegation from the Prosecutor's case is that Mr. Milutinovic has misled the National Assembly. It has been raised, it has been read in the court yesterday --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: -- and the professor was there. I'm not calling for speculation; I'm just calling for his opinion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There are matters of fact within the -- statements of fact within his submissions such as the discussions were only about troops or a new Gauleiter would govern Kosovo and"they led us to Rambouillet to strangle us in the dark." Now whose the judge of whether these are leading statements or not? Is that not what this is about rather than just to hear Professor Markovic give a general comment about the truthfulness of the witness in the context of that speech. Now, if there's any particular point you wish to challenge there and ask the witness specifically about, then that's what re-examination is for, but not that sort of general inquiry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So rephrase the approach to this, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I will move to another matter now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was a lot of talk about the letters that had been sent to representatives of Albanian majority parties and of course all other ethnic communities there, calling them to take part in negotiations. It was discussed at several points and I'm not going to reference each one of them. I would like to read to you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just before you proceed, it must be my diction again that's causing the problem, but I think I referred in what I said to you to three things that Mr. Milutinovic said in the meeting of the National Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Four, in fact: Troops, the new Gauleiter that would guide Kosovo, and I also mentioned "they led us to Rambouillet to strangle us in the dark" which has been omitted from the transcript. Anyway, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, we'll come back to this question of the Assembly of the 23rd of March a little later. I reminded you that there was a lot of discussion of the letters sent to the representatives of the ethnic communities and the national communities, including the representatives of the Albanian majority parties in Kosovo. Mr. Merovci testified here, and I would like to read part of his testimony for you to comment on. I'll read it in English, as the transcript is in English and you will hear the interpretation of what I read out. It's on page 8497 asked: [In English] "Well, you must have known if you were working closely with Dr. Rugova that in 1998 Professor Markovic as head of this delegation had written to Dr. Rugova, and other Kosovar Albanian leaders to attend meetings with the Serb delegation to discuss these issues. You must have known that? "A. Yes. This is I know -- this I know because I received these invitations as a person responsible for protocol issues, but for your information I was involved mostly and primarily with technical issues, not with negotiations or political issues. And sometimes things developed so fast that I cannot always give you an answer. The fact is that I received these invitations and signed that I received these invitations. I don't deny it, I said." [Interpretation] And he goes on: [In English] "And you also must know in that same context that this delegation had invited the Kosovar Albanian leaders and had been refused at least 15 times. The Serbian delegation would come to Pristina and the Albanian delegation would not appear. You must know that? "A. Yes, I recall that." [Interpretation] And he goes on. [In English] "In answer to one of my questions, you said that the Albanian delegation refused to meet in the building of Serbian government in Pristina, but the Albanian Kosovar -- Kosovar Albanian leadership refused to meet anywhere. They wouldn't meet in Pristina, they wouldn't meet in Belgrade. They were invited to meet anywhere any time and they refused, correct?" And the answer: "The Albanian side always insisted on presence of international factors at such meetings." [Interpretation] Professor, a brief comment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's no way to conduct re-examination, Mr. Zecevic. That's a -- this is a submission you're making. This is evidence which contradicts the evidence that -- or at least it contradicts the approach that the Prosecution were taking in cross-examining Mr. Markovic, but it's not for Mr. Markovic to comment on that evidence. You can argue about it until the cows come home once we get to the end of the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, the letters you sent on behalf of the delegation of Serbia and the letters sent by President Milutinovic, were they based on your sincere wish to sit down and talk to the representatives of the Albanians or --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object in part because he may be able to speak to his sincere wish regarding the letters he sent, but he can't speak as to why Mr. Milutinovic sent the letters.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Okay. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The letters you wrote to the Albanians, inviting them to meetings, were they written with intention to actually sit down and talk to them or was it done only to show the international community that allegedly attempts were being made to do something about the situation?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The very fact that we did go to Pristina at the scheduled time and in the scheduled place speaks of the fact that we actually did implement this, that we actually did try to carry out our intention and meet those we had invited.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. Professor, I suggest we go back to the transcript of the 9th of August now. Please look at P993.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Just one second, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Tab 27. I apologise, Professor, it's in the grey binder. I do apologise. 27.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You remember that Mr. Hannis asked you about the fact that this document is dated the 31st of March, 1990, that this date is at the very end of the document?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And then you explained that the professional services of the secretariat would propose proposals, prepare proposals.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, do you allow for the possibility that this date, the 31st of March, 1999, is the date when the proposal was prepared in the ministry by that ministry's service?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's quite possible. I explained that this was the time of the air-strikes, that the ministries were dislocated, that the cabinet had its sessions not in its own building but in the building of the National Bank of Serbia. And in all that chaos, it's quite possible that there can be a discrepancy in the dates and it's possible that this is the date when the service for normative affairs in the Ministry of the Interior drew up the draft of this decree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Does that mean both acts would occur on the same day, the promulgation by the president and the presentation of the document to him for his consideration?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honours, the evidence so far is that on the -- there was a government session on the 6th, the document which was sent by Mr. -- by Professor Markovic as vice-president -- as a vice prime minister -- as deputy prime minister of the government to President Milutinovic is dated on the 6th. And the document is, as you can see, it's published on the 7th of April, 1999. The problem that Mr. Hannis has seen and was questioning Professor was that the -- in the contents of the decree, it says at the very end "31st of March, 1999," and that is what I am exploring right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, in any case, the decree enters into force in this case on the date of its publication in the Official Gazette?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the 7th of April, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So regardless of the fact that the date in the document is the 31st of March, 1999, this decree began to be enforced only after the 7th of April, 1999?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As of the 7th of April, 1999, onwards. It entered into force as soon as it was published, which means that from that time onwards it was enforced.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Professor -- just a moment. This is the 10th of August, so in the transcript on page 13291 to 13296 there was testimony about the powers of the president to refuse to promulgate a decree proposed to him by the government or submitted to him by the government. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis suggested that there might be a theoretical possibility that the president on the one hand issue a decree according to his own will in one way, and then the next day the government might ask him to promulgate a decree contrary to what had been promulgated the day before. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And you said that the government had absolute executive power under the constitution. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's not what I say; it's what the constitution says. The 1990 constitution in Article 9, paragraph 3, and I only paraphrased it. So Article 9, paragraph 3 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Let's get to the question, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, as the government has executive power under the constitution, in your opinion could the president refuse to promulgate a decree during a state of war, thereby blocking the work of the cabinet or to issue decrees contrary to the position of the cabinet?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The president acts in compliance with the constitution if he makes it possible for each branch of the government to carry out its powers, the parliament legislative powers, the government executive powers, and that is why he signs these decrees. The president of the republic acts in compliance with the constitution when he makes it possible for all the various branches of government to carry out their particular competencies.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. At one point you said that in your opinion if the president were to appoint a prime minister designate who does not have a majority in the Assembly, that this could be contrary to the spirit of the constitution?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely, because he knows in advance that such a candidate cannot put together a government, put together a cabinet and cannot be elected. And in this way he is protracting the proceedings, delaying the appointment of the government, the cabinet.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you see an analogy between these two situations, Professor, if the president should propose a candidate who has a majority and if he fails to do so would it be contrary to the spirit of the constitution; and also, if the president were to refuse to promulgate a decree and thus block the work of the cabinet, that would also be contrary to the spirit of the constitution, would it not?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, one might say or one might take it as being contrary to the spirit of the constitution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, on page 13304, there was mention of Article 135 of the Constitution of Serbia and its function. And Mr. Hannis suggested that it was unconstitutional for the commission to draw up a constitution contrary to the Constitution of the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia, and then you explained the reasons why this was necessary. Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, do you remember that the Republic of Slovenia after the amendments you spoke about, the ones of 1989, introducing the supremacy of the republican constitution over the federal constitution issued a declaration on the sovereignty of the Republic of Slovenia as early as the 6th of July, 1990?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was a judge of the Constitutional Court at the time and we had to evaluate the constitutionality of that declaration.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, do you remember that Croatia on the 5th of September adopted a law structuring its republican administration and establishing the foreign ministry of Croatia and the Ministry of Defence of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and that law was also evaluated for constitutionality by the Constitutional Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, do you recall that the Croatian constitution of 1990 also contained an article, saying that Croatia would remain part of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia until a new agreement is reached with other federal units, that is, republics that were part of the Federation, or until otherwise decided by the Croatian parliament?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that constitution of Croatia of 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Did you have all these facts in mind when you wrote the 1990 Constitution of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. I tried to put all that to the esteemed Prosecutor, although that provision of the constitution which was legally questionable was justified for those reasons. It does not question the Federation at all. Since other republics were announcing secession, it contained this defensive clause; namely, what would happen with Serbia if secession happens.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would need the guidance from the Trial Chamber in this matter. The Professor was asked by Your Honours and my learned colleague about the composition of the constitutional commission, and Professor confirmed that he would be able to refresh his memory if he saw it because it has been published in the Official Gazette. I have -- I have this Official Gazette, Your Honours, now. Would you like me to show this to Professor?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The constitutional commission for the constitution of 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't have any objection. I question the relevance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, very well, we'll allow you to --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I mean, I'm not -- I thought that it was of the interest of the Trial Chamber and that is why we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is it in e-court?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, it's not yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I needed some guidance from Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Should we give it an IC number, is that the easiest way of dealing with it?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be IC134, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please don't just ask the Professor to read it. If it's some -- if all you're wanting is to furnish the names to us, then it's in now as an item in the process and you can refer to it, if necessary, in due course.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, is that the decision you spoke about?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: We see from that decision that, as you said, the president was Dr. Zoran Sokolovic, vice-president was Mr. Vucetic?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've told all that to Mr. Hannis --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is there a purpose to this question other than to give us the names?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's what I said. We've got it now. You don't need to ask the Professor to read the names out to us as we can read for ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, if you could just tell us about -- one of the questions asked by the Judges concerned the composition of this commission in terms of ethnic affiliation. Were there any members of the Albanian community and other ethnic communities that lived in Serbia; and if so, could you at least give us one or two names?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We see from here that it had two sources of membership. One was the Assembly, there were MPs, and there were also members coming from the scientific and expert community. I, for instance, was elected member of the constitutional commission as a university professor. If we are to judge by names, there are some Albanians, Ahmeti Bahadrin [phoen], I'm sorry if I'm mispronouncing, then Rexhep Hoxha.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You don't need to go through the whole list.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say judging by the names that they are Albanians. If you gave me some more time maybe I could find more, but you can see that it's a body with several dozen members, as I've said to the learned Prosecutor, so that constitutional commission was composed of several dozen people, as we can see from the list.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, on page 13332 you spoke about the wording of the presidential oath as defined in the Constitution of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Does this solemn oath affect in any way the way the president discharges his functions under Article 83?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Has that question not been answered?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't think, Your Honour. I don't think it has been answered, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Our recollection is that it has, but we do not want to deprive you of an opportunity to give us information we don't already have. So you can answer the question, Professor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, very briefly, that oath means that the president of the republic in discharging his functions under Article 83 as well as 84 and 85, 89, and 132, paragraph 1 of the constitution, would be guided by the values indicated in the oath: Peace, prosperity of the citizens, integrity of the territory, the sovereignty of the state, respect for civil and other rights, observation of the law and the constitution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: On page 13337, you spoke of the authority of the president in response to a question from my learned friend. You explained that, in your view, a president who is at the same time a leader of a large party has much greater authority than a president who is not a party leader. Could you explain that at greater length because I don't think we have that on the transcript?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's self-explanatory. A party leader gets more exposure; he embodies the party he leads. When we say "the party," we see the face of the party leader, that's the association. A president in office who is not a party leader certainly has less authority than one who is, and that is partly because major political decisions are made by agreement between major party leaders who personify their parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. At several points on Friday, beginning with 13349, 13371 and 73 you explained your positions concerning the Supreme Defence Council and you gave your explanation of the relations between Articles 135 and 136 of the constitution and, for instance, Article 4 of the Law on Defence. And you said, or rather, I'd like to ask this. Based on Article 4 of the Law on Defence, if you would be so kind as to open it. Shall I give you the tab number?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Just bear with me, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me help you, it's 62.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Professor, Article 4, pursuant to the provisions of this article which stipulates the procedure for proclaiming one of the emergency situations, does the army automatically get engaged only under the provisions of Article 4 in such situations?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not said anywhere in that article. The article deals only with the criteria that the Federal Assembly must be guided by when proclaiming one of the three degrees of emergency. The article does not mention the use of the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Article 4 gives discretion to the Federal Assembly in proclaiming one of the emergency situations, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the Federal Assembly evaluates and decides whether the conditions are there, whether the necessary prerequisites are there, to proclaim one of the four irregular or emergency situations.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object. That misstates what the document itself says. It has discretion to determine where the condition exist, but the language of the law itself says they shall proclaim an emergency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's clear to us, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I didn't want to go into that because it is in the text of the law as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please remember that the purpose of re-examination is to correct anything you think may have been misrepresented through cross-examination and to supplement your own case to the extent that it may have been challenged by cross-examination. It's not a re-hash of your own case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, in the course of your evidence on page 13306 -- sorry, 386, when you were cross-examined by Mr. Hannis, you were shown a letter written by General Perisic. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If I understood your position correctly as you stated it, it is that decisions of the Supreme Defence Council are political conclusions and positions and that formal enactments are later made on their basis?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are you going to challenge something that the witness has said --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- or try and correct something that the witness has said or are you simply asking him to repeat what he said already?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, he has been shown a document by my learned friend --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, but you see if you look at your question you'll see my concern. "If I understood your position correctly as you stated it, it says these are political" -- now, that is not an appropriate question for re-examination. You have to get to the point straight away that you think has been misrepresented in some way or get to the point that you think will help to counter something that emerged in cross-examination. But don't please ask the witness to just repeat what he's already said.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, I would like to show you document 4D137.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Could we have 4D137.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not sure this is an exhibit that was on the list that was going to be used with the witness and I'm not sure how it arises from cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, Mr. Hannis produced the letter from General Perisic and invited -- invited Professor to comment on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And is it 4D137?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, no, that is not. Now, this document is the directive from General Perisic issued on the 28th of July, which is closely connected to the letter which he sent in -- which was presented to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, what is it you say the witness can help with on this point? Remember you've got 4D137 -- or, of course, it hasn't -- or is it in fact introduced into the case yet?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It was introduced into the case, I think Mr. Ackerman introduced it when we were talking to General Vasiljevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: But it is our opinion that it arised out of cross.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Indeed, but is there something that the witness can say about this document that will assist us that you can't just say in your submissions in due course. Is there some point of knowledge that he has about this directive?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I never showed the document to the witness, so that is what -- I mean, I can do that in submission as well, Your Honour, that is -- the document speaks for itself, and I'm not -- I'm pretty sure that the witness has never seen the document before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. Well, we will note that you are relying on that document and you will be able to make submissions about it. But if there is something you think the witness can cast light on from his particular position, either through knowledge of fact or his expertise, then you should ask him. But that should be a pointed question that focuses on the particular issue that you think he can deal with.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Okay. Just one second. Please bear with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I suggest that this witness won't be able to help on this document. He's told us he's no expert on military matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, I appreciate that, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: We'll move on to something else, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, on the 13th of August, on page 13406, we spoke, or rather, Mr. Hannis asked you about decisions of the Supreme Defence Council. At one point Mr. Hannis said on page 13406 if two members, for example, President Milutinovic and President Milosevic, were present, they can conduct business and adopt decisions without President Djukanovic and it doesn't really matter how serious President Djukanovic's objection is, simply President Milutinovic votes together with President Milosevic and President Djukanovic will in any case be out-voted. Do you remember that statement by the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, tell me, is it correct that the only two conclusions, or rather, that on the 9th of June and the 4th of October conclusions were adopted by a consensus?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it follows from the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, look at the session of the 24th of November, 1998, it's P1576. I'll try and find the tab number now. It's dated the 24th of November, 1998.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Tab 56.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. Professor, please tell me something. At sessions of the Supreme Defence Council was a vote taken on the replacement of General Perisic or not?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, or at least that's what follows from the minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, would you be so kind as to read out the last page of these minutes in the Serbian language. It's the last three paragraphs beginning with the words: "President Milosevic ..." Please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What is the purpose of this? Are you disputing the translation? Because we can certainly read what's been translated for us. Are you going to ask a question or what?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm going to ask Professor to comment on this after he reads it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just in general terms or have you got a particular question you want to ask him?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I have to ask -- I have a particular question to ask Professor in relation to this statement of President Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, it doesn't need to be read out for that. Ask your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, you see on this last page in the first paragraph President Milosevic says that some issues were being raised at sessions of the Supreme Defence Council which are not within the competence of that organ?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he says they are --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There's no question in there that this witness needs to answer for you. What's the question you need to ask the witness? And unless you start focusing on that, Mr. Zecevic, I will have to bring your re-examination to an end.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You cannot just ask him to read -- we can read this for ourselves. Is there some particular question you need his expertise on? I assume he wasn't there, so it's not the fact itself you want the evidence on. Please focus a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, at this session no vote was taken on the replacement of General Perisic. He was replaced by an ordinance of the president, and at the next session, that's tab 57 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, what is the question? What is the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I will withdraw that question, Your Honour. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, on page 13415 when asked by my learned friend, Mr. Hannis, about the rules of procedure of the Supreme Defence Council of 1998, which state that before the changes of March 1999 President Milosevic was the one who proposed the agenda, was he not? Professor, did this situation change after the rules of procedure of 1999?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we see that the same provision remained, the one that had been in the 1992 rules of procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, with respect to this provision and the right to convene meetings, did anything change between 1992 and 1999 in the two rules of procedure of those years?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only thing that changed was that now the federal minister for defence could also convene meetings, as could the Chief of the General Staff, whereas in 1992 it was only a member of the Supreme Council and, of course, the president of the Supreme Defence Council on his own initiative and that is ex officio the president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. In other words, the number of people who could convene meetings was extended, it was broadened. Two others were added, the federal minister of defence and they Chief of the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In any case, it's the president who schedules the meetings. Did this fact change between 1992 and 1999, the two rules?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you see, that seems to contradict what's just been said. The only thing that -- the last answer was: "The only thing that changed was that now the federal minister of defence could also convene meetings, as could the Chief of the General Staff ..." And you asked: "In any case, it's the president who schedules the meetings. Did this fact change between 1992 and 1997 [sic] ..." And the answer is no and these two answers are not consistent.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I see, Your Honour, but I wasn't able to follow the translation as well. The Professor gave a perfectly right answer in Serbian because he said the federal minister of defence could ask for a meeting to be convened, and that is the change that the number of people who can ask the president to convene the meeting has become bigger. That is the only change.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That now --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: But the president in any case is the only one who can call up the meetings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In English that now makes sense. Thank you, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I wasn't able to follow it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's not your fault. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, on page 13422 ...

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: My learned friend showed you a document marked P2166, and these are minutes of the inter-ministerial staff for the suppression of terrorism. And I think you said that you had never seen this document before and that you had no comments on it except when asked whether in the constitution there is a provision envisaging the existence of such an organ. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, I have to refresh your memory now. On the 30th of July, we commented on this document, you and I, and do you remember we --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We may have a problem if Mr. Zecevic was the only person present. He's turning himself into a possible witness in this case if the Professor disagrees, then he's either going to have to live with the answer or turn into a witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, no doubt he'll live with the answer, but that suggests you're withdrawing your objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, I maintain my objection, Your Honour. Unless there was a third party present, there's a potential problem I see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, but it's a problem we're perfectly capable of dealing with, should it emerge as a problem. Just be careful, Mr. Zecevic, how you approach this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I am, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It would be helpful, I think, if you were to ask more open questions rather than put the answers in the witness's mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, can you tell me, if you remember these minutes, what the character of this body was?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't remember having seen this document before. I studied the stenographic record and the minutes from the meetings of the Supreme Defence Council, but these minutes weren't among those documents and I cannot remember having seen this document. As for the character --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just a moment, how does the question of the character arise out of cross-examination? I assume Mr. Hannis departed from that question of the witness after he said he had not seen the document before.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, no, but the question -- the question by Mr. Hannis was: "Is there any provision in the constitution for that kind of body?" That was the question by Mr. Hannis on page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And the answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And the answer is: "No, we have seen that there are several provisions, six articles, but no such body is mentioned in the constitution."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And you're going to challenge that now, are you?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, not actually challenge that it's not in the constitution, but to explain the nature of this body. But Professor doesn't remember it, so I will move on from this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: -- because there is no point. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, although you don't recall that document, Mr. Hannis took you through it. And at one point he asked you as regards the other political personages present, do you know what their affiliation was, what party they belonged to, Mr. Milosevic, Milutinovic, Minic, Sainovic, and he suggested that they were members of the SPS and you said yes. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, well, I told him the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I agree. Professor, did these persons hold any state offices, apart from being members of this party?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, but as far as I can remember the Prosecutor did not ask about that. He only asked whether they were members of the socialist party of Serbia, and my answer was yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In your opinion, was it the offices they held or their membership of the party that was the decisive factor in their attending the meeting?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, of course, it was the offices they held --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object this calls for speculation on the part of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What is the basis for the witness giving an opinion on this?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I read the part of the -- of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You have asked him to give an opinion on what would lead to their being appointed to this. Now, on what expertise of his do you rely for that question?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: On common sense, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, if it's common sense, well, you can address us at the end of the case on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I should point out I did ask a specific question about Mr. Matkovic who was listed as having no office other than being vice-president of the SPS. I did ask a question about him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you want to deal with that?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Matkovic is of no concern to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, during that same piece of testimony, Mr. Hannis showed you part of the minutes containing the word "Decision" with a capital D. Do you remember talking about that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I would be grateful if you were show it to me in order to refresh my memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That's page 3 in Serbian underlined tab 49, page 3, the passage that's underlined.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And for the record, this is Exhibit P2166.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: P2166, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 3.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Page 3, yes, I got it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You discussed that Decision, with capital D, do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, you agreed with comments made by my learned friend, but these are minutes, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we see the heading: "Minutes."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, minutes are made on the basis of some notes, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Minutes reflect what transpired at the session, at the appropriate session of that body.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The person who is speaking in that passage, is he referring to a decision with a small d or a capital D?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see a capital D and that's what the Prosecutor asked me about, if I recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object, that's not appropriate. I move to strike that answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There's no one speaking if that's an accurate translation of the answer. Someone's writing and he's written with a capital D.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, but it is -- the problem is that the person who is allegedly reporting is not making a reference to a capital O or a small o, and the person who is writing is somebody completely different. So he might use the capital O for no reason whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This is something you can argue about in due course. The witness knows nothing about the document --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I know, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- and the circumstances in which it was drawn up so he's not in a position to answer the question in any way that would assist us. He may have his views, but what matters is how we interpret the document in due course in light of the evidence of people who can actually talk about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I was just of the opinion that since Mr. Hannis was asking him about the small d or the capital D, that I'm entitled to do the same. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the course of cross-examination, Mr. Hannis on page 13438 read out to you part of the interview given General Pavkovic, P949. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In order to use the same references and ask you to comment on the same passages as the Prosecutor, I would like to use the same references 13 -- P1319 admitted into evidence in October 2006, and that's the interview of General Pavkovic dated 20th October 2000. I will read it out in English and you will get an interpretation. [In English] "Pavkovic: Well" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, just before you do that, remind me of the page --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Presiding Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Remind me, please, of the page at which this appears in cross-examination. 438, did you say?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It is page, Your Honour, 13438, and for the benefit of my learned friends across the way I intend to be reading from the interview which is Exhibit P949 and so on and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What is the question you're going to ask the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to ask the witness to -- I have to read him this article first so I can ask a question on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, no, tell me the question before you do because we're wasting an awful lot of time with inappropriate questions that take an eternity to be formulated.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I want to have a comment of the witness on this particular passage of Mr. Pavkovic's interview.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is that something he has an expertise on bearing in mind that he said he has no military expertise?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Definitely, Your Honour, because it talks about the role of the Supreme Defence Council and that is why I seek his opinion on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I mean, we have an example, for example: "I do not know the military doctrine and maybe these names and agencies are in keeping with the military doctrine."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: He says he believes --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The particular passage -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: He says he believes the constitutional provision is unequivocal and is echoed in the Law on the Army of Yugoslavia. Now what is it you're challenging in all that?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm challenging the existence of the Supreme Command, I'm challenging the fact that Mr. Milutinovic was on the Supreme Command and -- I mean, these are at least the first two which I'm challenging from this part which was read in the court yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have some confusion about what is proceeding here because I understood Mr. Zecevic to make a reference to Exhibit P1319 which was not an exhibit, I believe, which was not an exhibit on their list. And it's a television programme with callers calling in with questions for General Pavkovic. And I'm not sure how that relates to General Pavkovic's interview with the OTP, which is Exhibit 949 which is the one I used to ask the Professor questions about the Supreme Command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So what is it you're up to here, Mr. Zecevic? I'm not understanding what's going on. Please make it clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, it came out from the cross-examination because Mr. Hannis used the P949. The other document, the other interview by General Pavkovic is P1319, which is completely different from the one which Mr. Hannis was reading in court. Now, I want to read this interview to the Professor so he can give me his expert opinion on the views taken by General Pavkovic in this interview, like he did with the -- with Mr. Prosecutor, the very same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, the issue remains of why this wasn't included in your list of exhibits to be referred to.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I could have never anticipated that Mr. Hannis will use P949 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Was that not --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: -- in cross-examination --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Was that not on his list?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Was that not on his list of exhibits to be used?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was, Your Honours, but he provided the list of the documents he intends to use at the cross-examination the moment when our -- when our witness was sworn. I mean, that was the rule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Did you notify him last night that you were going to use it?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Why not? Well, would courtesy not have --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would that not have been a reasonable courtesy to extend to --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, definitely, Your Honour, it is an oversight on my part, but I thought that Mr. Hannis -- this is a document which is admitted already, P1319. I would assume that if he quoted the P949 he would have had this also in his perspective while preparing for cross-examination. I really -- I'm sorry that I didn't notify Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we'll allow you to proceed, Mr. Zecevic, but I hope that you have pointed questions which the witness is in a position to assist us in relation to.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: "Pavkovic: Well, I was criticised a lot because allegedly I was the first one that used the expression (supreme commander). Of course, until that time that had not bothered anyone. After the aggression against our country and the well-known events regarding the stabilisation of the units of the Yugoslav Army in conditions when they had destroyed installations, when they did not have an existing infrastructure, it was completely logical that in certain moments we use that term." That's page 4 of the English text. That's second paragraph. "You know" -- Your Honours, for your reference, it's page 4, second paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It starts with: "Pavkovic ... "

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, we have it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: "You know the Supreme Defence Council is an advisory body which is called for by the Constitution, and it actually, as its name says, gives advice before a decision is made. But as a collective body it cannot issue executive orders. The president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia issues executive orders. And that is the principle of seniority and subordination in the army. Orders on deploying certain units cannot be issued collectively. For example, the Supreme Defence Council made a decision to defend the country in case of NATO attack. That was only a" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You've read enough for the question -- for any question to be asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We don't want the history of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yeah, but, Your Honours, I just have two more --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Oh, well, go on then if you think it's necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: "That was the only decision that the defence council made, but commanding, issuing orders for deployment of units is carried out by that one man" --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, a transcript matter. The exhibit reads: "That was only a decision" not the only decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: "That was only a decision that the defence council made."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, you heard this passage, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have, like everyone here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, is there such a term as the -- as "supreme commander" in the constitution?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, the constitution says the Army of Yugoslavia is commanded in wartime and peacetime --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What are you asking him that we haven't heard before?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, can you agree with General Pavkovic that the Supreme Defence Council was a consulting body?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is my qualification. I've said that precisely many times.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, the witness has said that several times to us. What is it -- please ask him something from this that's new.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, does the constitution know the term "Supreme Command"?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's -- you're asking a question you've just already asked and which has been asked several times before.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What is it that's new in here that you want to hear?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That is completely contradictory to what we have heard yesterday in the court which was read by Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, but the Professor said earlier that there is no such name in the constitution. What Pavkovic said in that interview is not evidence against your client. We've made that clear. The only relevance of his interview in your case is that Mr. Hannis can put the terms and ask a witness whether he agrees or disagrees, and it's only what the witness says that is relevant evidence against your client. And the witness has said that there was no such concept in the constitution as the Supreme Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, but that is the part of the direct -- of the direct that he -- Professor said that there is no term of supreme commander, Supreme Command, and anything like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The question arose in the cross-examination where -- when Mr. Hannis read the -- read the interview of General Pavkovic where general says there is a Supreme Command. Now I'm asking the Professor again. Maybe he --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But did the Professor accept as a result of that that there was such a body?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, he wasn't asked that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Then there is no evidence against you. What is the evidence -- the actual evidence from Professor Markovic that you don't like that you're trying to re-examine on?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I just felt that it has not been substantial -- sufficiently explained. That was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I certainly disagree with you. I wonder if my colleagues require to hear more on this. Give us a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, one of my colleagues in this Tribunal, not on this Bench, regularly describes the purpose of re-examination as to rehabilitate the witness or rehabilitate the evidence. In other words, to deal with any damage to your case that has been done by cross-examination. Now, that's not what you're doing at the moment. You're re-emphasising points that have already been made by the witness on which he hasn't been shaken in cross-examination, and these are things you can do in the submissions you make in due course. It doesn't help us to hear several times from the witness the same answer. Now, if you think that he was undermined, that he gave an answer that undermined your position, then you can ask him about that. But if all you're doing is saying: Well, here's another example that you can read and tell us yet again the same thing as you told the Prosecutor, then that's not appropriate in re-examination. It should be a focused exercise dealing with particular issues that were the subject of cross-examination to your disadvantage. Now, could you please follow that guidance in proceeding further with your re-examination. If it helps, we'll break early, if you like, and resume at quarter past.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: I think the best will be that you took some time and gave it a thought and while you have your coffee, that is better way.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And we'll resume at 11.15. Professor, could you please leave again with the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [The witness takes the stand].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, I have one more question for you. On page 13438 in response to a question from my learned friend Mr. Hannis about the transition of the army at the point of -- in time when the war was declared, according to the constitution and the Law on Defence and the Law on the Army, is there a change of status in the organisation of the army at the point in time when war is declared or in any type of state of emergency?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Staying only in the sphere of the law, there are no such changes. There is no such transformation either in the title, in the constitution, or in the appropriate laws which regulate the field of the defence of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. We have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zecevic. Yes, Professor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like you to take into account that any inappropriate address of the Court is just a consequence of being ignorant of the court protocol and nobody informed me of it previously. So I would just like to offer my apologies if I had misaddressed you in any way. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What has happened in this case does not concern me in the least, and you have to need to apologise for anything as far as I'm concerned. And I don't see any particular concern on the part of my colleagues. Some might take a different view about the protocol that should be followed in court, but I think we as a Bench consider the appropriate overriding protocol to follow is that of politeness, and that has certainly been the position you've taken. So please don't concern yourself on that score.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: I just appreciate what you said at the end. That was nice wrapping-up. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Judge Nosworthy has a question for you, Professor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Yes, Professor Markovic, with the leave of my Presiding Judge, I wanted to discover from you if there is any provision within the constitution or any other relevant provision that would provide for compelling a public officer or a body to perform a public duty that they were obliged to perform but did not perform. Is there any such provision in place? It would be equivalent to - I don't know if you're familiar with the orders in some common-law jurisdiction, that is an order of mandamus to compel a public officer or body to perform a duty, a specific duty, that they have, whether under statute or the constitution or otherwise and that which has not been performed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In our constitution that was in effect at that time and in the present constitution, there is no such provision. That is because our constitutions and the entire legislature is drafted in the tradition of European continental law and not in the tradition of Anglo-Saxon law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Professor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Professor, that completes your evidence. Some people think that this Trial Chamber follows a demanding trial schedule, so thank you for finding the resilience to bear with us as we endeavour to make progress and thank you for surviving each day intact able to return and continue until this stage, I think eight or nine days. We appreciate also that you've been here before. This, hopefully, will be your last appearance here; I can't guarantee that. I have no idea what may yet follow. But for what you have contributed to the Tribunal so far, we thank you. You are now free to leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, our next witness is Mr. Zivota Cosic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Before we start, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: While it's distributed, we have the -- we will have to amend the notifications for Mr. Cosic, that is, his supplemental information sheet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Which is 1D762.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It is just a certain two changes in his 92 ter statement which he recognised on proofing session held on 6th of August, 2007. And it is attached at the end of his 92 ter statement under tab 1 as the very last page. Our friends from the Prosecutor's office have been notified about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Some time ago -- I mean, immediately after it happened. That's one thing. And our -- the witness after this, Mr. Kojic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we can deal with that at the time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, no, I'm waiting on the witness coming in.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I was wonder if you would ask if I objected to that application but I have no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you should have done so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please take the witness out.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, no, none.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are you objecting to it?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: None. I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, I assumed if you didn't rise, that there was no objection. Thank you. Good morning, Mr. Cosic. Could you please make the solemn declaration to speak the truth by reading aloud the document which will now be placed before you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. You will now be examined by Mr. Zecevic, who is on your left. Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, may we provide the witness with his binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good day, Mr. Cosic.

utterances.speaker: ZIVOTA COSIC
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Cosic, for the transcript can you please give us your full name.

utterances.speaker: ZIVOTA COSIC
utterances.text: My name is Zivota Cosic, son of Miroslav.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Cosic, you were minister of industry in the Government of the Republic of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOTA COSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us when you served in that post?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOTA COSIC
utterances.text: I was a minister in the Government of the Republic of Serbia I think from March 1997 until approximately mid-March 1998, when I became in the second government of Mirko Marjanovic, the minister for energy in the Government of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Cosic, you provided President Milutinovic's Defence with a statement on the 29th of June and then with another statement or an additional statement on the 6th of August, 2007, when you changed two paragraphs from your previous statement from the 29th of June. Can you please look at tab number 1, that is the first document. And can you please tell us whether that is your statement and the amendment you made of the 6th of August.

utterances.speaker: ZIVOTA COSIC
utterances.text: Yes, both of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You looked over these statements before you entered the courtroom, during the past 24 hours I mean? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOTA COSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Are these the two statements and are the contents of the statements accurate, do they reflect the truth of the events described therein according to your best recollection?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOTA COSIC
utterances.text: My statement, according to my recollection, does reflect the situation we were in from the 23rd of March until the 15th or the 16th of June, when the aggression on our country ended.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Cosic, if you were asked the same questions as while you were giving the statement, would your answers be the same?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOTA COSIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have nothing more to state or to add. That's what I said and I stand by it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
