utterances.text: Mr. Cosic, just one short warning. Every time that I complete my question, please pause so that it can be interpreted and so that we do not overlap.

utterances.speaker: ZIVOTA COSIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Cosic, you said that you were a minister in the government in 1997?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOTA COSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Where were you before you became the minister?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOTA COSIC
utterances.text: I was the deputy minister for industry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Are the headphones all right now?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOTA COSIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So you were deputy minister, and where were you before you became deputy minister in the Government of the Republic of Serbia? Just wait, please. Please wait before you begin answering.

utterances.speaker: ZIVOTA COSIC
utterances.text: I was at the ministry for industry and I became deputy minister on the 1st of June 1993. At the time, the prime minister was Mr. Nikola Sainovic. And then the first government of Mirko Marjanovic, I remained in that government and I became deputy industry minister. Later when the government was reconstructed in March 1997, I was appointed deputy minister -- no, this was not in 1997, it was in 1994, in May. In March 1997, I became minister for industry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cosic, you started that answer by saying you became deputy minister in June 1993, then you said later May 1994 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: It was assistant minister in June 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, the interpreter -- it's okay. The interpreter has corrected the mistake. We can move on. Thank you. We have all this history --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I know that that particular point isn't in the history, but insofar as the history is relevant, I think we have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Cosic, since we provided your information in your statement, I'm just going to ask you about some details that you can help us with. Can you please tell me in paragraph 13 of your statement you say that you were aware of the seriousness of the NATO threats at the beginning of 1999 but you did not believe that the bombing would actually happen. Can you please explain to us, what was that conviction based on, yours and that of other citizens, and what sort of preparations were made for that?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOTA COSIC
utterances.text: I can state responsibly that in the government we did not expect the bombing to take place. The citizens that we met in the street in contacts with us didn't feel that way either. We were convinced that there would be a peaceful political solution for the crisis that we were in, and, of course, we did not make any plans. In this material, if you see only in the second half of May was I appointed deputy commander of civilian protection in the Government of the Republic of Serbia, and this was already the end of the bombing on our country. Had we known that that would happen, we would have probably made some preparations, but nobody sensible could conceive that somebody would pull the trigger on a country which in its entire history never committed aggression towards anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Cosic, in the statement that you gave, you say that after the start on the 23rd of March you were given an assignment by the prime minister to relocate hazardous materials. In paragraph 15, you talk about the problem presented by Prva Iskra from Baric and how -- and what you undertook in that respect. Can you please explain to us a little bit the scale of the problem that you were facing and the potential consequences that a strike would have on this factory, this particular factory.

utterances.speaker: ZIVOTA COSIC
utterances.text: I want to say first that a meeting took place in the Government of Serbia on the 23rd of March at 11.30. The meeting was chaired by the late Prime Minister, Mirko Marjanovic, and the meeting was attended by the Deputy Prime Minister Dragomir Tomic, Deputy Prime Minister Nikola Sainovic, and myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: All of that is in your statement.

utterances.speaker: ZIVOTA COSIC
utterances.text: And I want to say next that we looked at all the factories that were located near large cities because we knew that if there -- the bombing did take place, it would cause a lot of damage to the citizens and the towns itself. It was up to me to deal with Prva Iskra Baric to deal with the question of relocating the hydrochloric acid from there. I must say that it was a very difficult job because even the thought by the engineers from Prva Iskra to have to relocate the hydrochloric acid was something very difficult but they were forced to do it. I was forced to address President, Mr. Milutinovic and also Mr. Nikola Sainovic. I had talks with each one of them about how to resolve this problem. I knew this: President Milutinovic can influence. When our railways were questioned to enable priority transportation means in order to transport hazardous materials. Secondly, Deputy Prime Minister of the federal government Nikola Sainovic was also a mining and energy minister before me and I know that he was also one of the directors from the smelting and mining complex Bor and that they had great capacities to resolve the question of relocating the hydrochloric acid. I asked him to get in touch with the institute for nuclear technology from Vinca to ask the director, I think his name was Milosevic, for them to find a solution and that I and Mr. President, Mr. Milutinovic, could find a way to relocate the hydrochloric acid. Of course at the time, the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia did not have such cisterns constructed of special low-carbon steel which could transport an acid of that type. We tried to resolve that question abroad. Of course we did not get permission for that because the country was isolated, it was bombed, so we had to take cisterns from our Energogas to prepare them specially, to decontaminate them and then transport them via the railways to the Nikola Tesla thermal hydro-electric power-plant in Obrenovac and then there was the problem of how to cover the 10 kilometres from Obrenovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You said all of that in your statement. I'm interested in the following: What sort of consequences would a hit on the Prva Iskra plant in Baric have had?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOTA COSIC
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's in the statement as well, so -- this is the death of several tens of thousands of citizens or is it something else that you're dealing with?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, it is something that came up that Mr. Cosic was giving a comment just the other day. So that's what I'm trying to elicit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Okay. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Go ahead. What would the scale of the consequences of a hit on Prva Iskra Baric have had?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOTA COSIC
utterances.text: I'll be very brief. It would have been equivalent to the dropping of a small atomic bomb for the citizens of Belgrade. I have to tell you that when Lap was installed in Prva Iskra Baric they wanted to introduce some new technology but they gave up the idea because of the danger it would pose for the town, for the city, and the citizens were afraid and they were right. I have to tell you that when we were relocating this hydrochloric acid, Baric, the place where the factory was located, was a ghost town. Everybody left. Half of the town of Obrenovac left. Although, under international conventions nobody with any common sense at all would have dared bomb such a factory, but when we saw what was happening and that it might really happen, we decided to relocate this dangerous material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, is Baric a name of a company or a name of a place?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It is both, Your Honours. The name of the place is Baric and the name of the factory is Prva Iskra Baric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And the second sentence of paragraph 15 is accurate, is it, that they were not authorised to store the hydrochloric acid?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, the wording in Serbian is different. The Prva Iskra Baric did not have a clue what to do with the stored acid. No, the translation is wrong, Your Honour. Maybe -- maybe witness can help.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think you should ask him to read that sentence from his copy of the statement, and then it will be translated by the interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Would you please read out the first sentence of point 15.

utterances.speaker: ZIVOTA COSIC
utterances.text: "During work the biggest problem was caused by Prva Iskra from Baric which did not have a decision -- or it did not have a solution for the stored hydrochloric acid." They did not know how to relocate it, in other words.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Cosic, you were given the task of dealing with this issue from Prime Minister Marjanovic?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOTA COSIC
utterances.text: Yes, before that I had been minister for industry and regardless of the fact that in this second government I was in charge of mining in energy, I felt this was my moral obligation to deal with this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. Was it your moral obligation or were you given a task by the prime minister?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOTA COSIC
utterances.text: I was given a task by the prime minister because I was the one who knew best how to do that. I was one of the engineers who had participated in the construction of the cellulose plant, I knew quite a lot about hazardous chemicals, and I had been working in the Krusik factory for a long time so I knew what all this was about.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Cosic, you informed the Prime Minister of what steps you were taking?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOTA COSIC
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. I had to report to the prime minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You say in your statement that you met Mr. Milutinovic in 1993, that you became friends. How did it come about that you informed President Milutinovic about what was being done to relocate the hydrochloric acid from Prva Iskra Baric?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOTA COSIC
utterances.text: Well, first I have to say that the president, Mr. Milutinovic, was a citizen of Belgrade and he knew best what it would mean for the citizens of Belgrade not to relocate this hydrochloric acid. Secondly, he knew me well because in 1993 I went to Greece on behalf of my factory, Krusik from Valjevo to buy some new technology for producing tin cans, and then I dropped into the embassy to meet my ambassador and at that time it was Mr. Milan Milutinovic. And that was when we got to know one another and started socialising. And I have to say that I was responsible to the Prime Minister Mirko Marjanovic and the Assembly of the Republic of Serbia which appointed me for my work. I was not duty-bound to send any documents to him, and I could not have done that without Prime Minister Mirko Marjanovic knowing because every -- all posts had to go through him. But because I was a friend of Milan Milutinovic, I always met him halfway. And when he called me on the phone, I would always give him the information he needed and asked for. Or if he asked me to come and see me well, of course, I would go and see my president and give him information so that he would be up-to-date on everything that was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Cosic, when you say that everything went through Mr. Mirko Marjanovic, you mean that no document went out from the cabinet without the prime minister's approval. Is that what you meant to say?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOTA COSIC
utterances.text: Yes, for any letter to be sent from the cabinet, the prime minister would have to know about it. I think that's normal.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So these reports that you're talking about in paragraph 37, 1D706, which you delivered to President Milutinovic, Deputy Prime Minister Tomic, and you, these reports were sent to Mr. Marjanovic and he gave the approval that they be delivered to President Milutinovic?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOTA COSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Cosic, when we look at the list of these plants you looked at in paragraph 21 and a little earlier on, I see that almost all the factories from the territory of Serbia and the autonomous province of Vojvodina are listed. But it's well-known that in the autonomous province of Kosovo and Metohija there was some factories which had stores of these hazardous materials; for example, Akumulatori Trepca from Kosovo and so on and so forth. So what was done and who was in charge of things there.

utterances.speaker: ZIVOTA COSIC
utterances.text: Look at 1D706, it says there quite clearly: "The Republic of Serbia, Ministry for Protection of the Environment, of the 11th of May, 1999, where all the heads of districts" --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: What page is that in the document, please?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOTA COSIC
utterances.text: 1D706, the page before the last, or rather, no, it's in the middle.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, 9 or 8?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOTA COSIC
utterances.text: Well, it says here: "Bearing in mind that on the territory of your district there are plants with ammonia -- Klanica [as interpreted] and so on, we inform you that it is your duty to check once again that all measures have been taken to protect the environment," and it's signed by Milos Milosavljevic. So all the factories on the territory of the Republic of Serbia were taken into account because the Republic of Serbia is a unified territory and we made no distinction. However, we paid more attention to those factories which were more dangerous because they were built next to large towns, and then, of course, we were also concerned about Trepca and the sulfuric acid there which we also dislocated from Kosovska Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This document is on page 8, or rather, that's on page 8 of the translation of the document. If I understood you correctly, the heads of the districts were in charge of relocating these hazardous materials on the territories of their districts. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOTA COSIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were duty-bound to inform the Government of the Republic of Serbia whether they could deal with this on their own or whether they needed assistance from the relevant ministries, either in experts or funds or means of transport, whatever they lacked, the government was there to provide so that the problem could be solved as soon as possible because we were short of time. The air-strikes had already begun. The relocation of hazardous chemicals had not yet been done.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: After you completed this huge task of relocating this acid and the hazardous materials from other factories, in paragraphs 23 and 24, 25, and 26, you say that a problem arose when the NATO aeroplanes started hitting electrical power-plants, transmission stations, and so on. Can you sum up this situation?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOTA COSIC
utterances.text: I have to tell you that I'm an engineer and I'm not normally afraid, but when I arrived in the Obrenovac power-plant and saw this technological invasion for the first time, graphite fibres which were covering the transformer station, covering several thousand square metres, nothing had been damaged but the thermo-electric power-plant was like a ghost place. There was no electricity, nothing was functioning. I have to tell you that on those 12.000 square metres there are enumerable posts 25 metres high with high-voltage cables on them. And I thought about how to solve this problem. On the ground, I found a lot of things that I didn't know what they were. I put them in a bag to go to the institute to ask Mr. Nikola Sainovic to help me and for us to try to find a way of removing this problem, dealing with the problem. However, when I arrived home, I had big problems with my wife who wouldn't let me in with these little keys; she thought they might be radioactive. And then I put them in the corridor and I went to see Minister Babic the next day and he said please don't bring this in here it might kill us all, it might have been exposed to radiation. I had no choice I had to solve the problem and Mr. Nikola Sainovic helped me a lot in this respect. He found the appropriate institute which provided the solution as to how we could solve this and we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You said that in 27 that in mid-May -- on the 24th of May, rather, you went from a meeting with President Milutinovic together with Slobodan Babic. Was this in order to inform the president because he was friend of yours or was it a duty you and Mr. Babic had?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOTA COSIC
utterances.text: Well, this went beyond friendship. We felt the president of our republic should know what was going on because the electricity shortage meant that there was no water in homes, no running water. And once you did re-establish the power-supply, it would take many hours for the pressure to rise sufficiently in high-rise buildings. And then there was a problem of sewage as well. How could sewage be moved from one place to another because unless this could be solved there could be an epidemic in Belgrade which would be even worse than the air-strikes, and it could be fatal for the citizens of Belgrade. We spoke to the president about drawing up a list of priorities which we did and the little electricity we had in Belgrade at the time had to be prioritized in order for hospitals to continue operating so they could have enough electricity for urgent operations, surgery; then bakeries had to operate; we had to provide electric power for the few schools that remained open; also for the manufacture of medicines --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In these paragraphs about the damage to the electricity supply, is there reference to assistance from Mr. Sainovic at present?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In the reference to electric supply?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I don't believe so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And is that not what these questions relate to?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, I never mentioned Mr. Sainovic in this context.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry. Just give me a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Babic and -- President Milutinovic and Mr. Babic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah. He said that Mr. Sainovic had helped him get in touch with the institute. Now, we have that evidence in the statement in relation to the disposal of the hydrochloric acid.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But it doesn't feature in your statement in relation to the electricity problem and the possible radioactivity. Is this a separate institute or is it the same institute, do you know? If you look at page 56, line 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Will you answer, Mr. Cosic, briefly, to this question of Judge Bonomy?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOTA COSIC
utterances.text: I asked Mr. Nikola Sainovic whether that issue could be resolved by the institute for nuclear technologies. I don't know whom he consulted. All I know is that he told me when I came to that meeting with him at Jugometal that we should apply sprinkling with natrium hydroxide. That's what we did and it turned out to be the right thing to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's back to the hydrochloric acid. But we seem to have a --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Natrium is not the same thing as the acid. It's NaOH.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Could you look, please, Mr. Cosic at your statement and at paragraph 17. Now, am I right in thinking that that paragraph relates to the disposal of the hydrochloric acid?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, we are talking about two different things. One is the removal of hydrochloric acid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just answer my question and we'll get to the solution. Am I correct in thinking that paragraph 17 is dealing with hydrochloric acid? No. Is that wrong?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes -- no. That -- I mean the paragraph 17 applies to hydrochloric acid. Removal of that acid and relocation of the Prva Iskra Baric factory is one thing. The second issue is Elektroprivreda and the relocation of Elektroprivreda with those fibres. We sprinkled the fibres with natrium hydroxide while they were laid out on the ground.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, where is that dealt with in your statement? Which paragraph should I be looking at?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That is -- Your Honour, if I may be of help, it is not in the statement. It's just what the witness said right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You see, we have got the issue of the hydrochloric acid. You know that -- maybe I try to make things too simple, Mr. Zecevic, but I had identified in here what I thought were two major issues. One was the disposal of hydrochloric acid; the other was dealing with the problems caused because of bomb damage to electricity and --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That is exactly right --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- and related things. And I get the impression that this matter of the fibres is to do with the electricity.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What I'm trying to be clear about is whether there is yet another occasion other than in paragraph 17 when the witness calls on the assistance of Mr. Sainovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: There is no such paragraph after --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, I know there's no paragraph, but what I'd like to know is whether it was another occasion because it's a much later event, isn't it, it's in May.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So I'm trying to find out if he had to call on the assistance of Mr. Sainovic twice and whether the institute is the same one or a different one because in the statement it's the institute for nuclear and other raw materials and I think in his evidence he's called it the institute for nuclear technology or something of that nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Would you like me to ask --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I would like that clarified, if possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Cosic, you heard the question. Did you seek the assistance of Mr. Sainovic in relation to the graphite fibres that were thrown on to the electrical installation in May 1999; and if you did, what assistance did he extend and which institute dealt with this? Please give me a concise answer.

utterances.speaker: ZIVOTA COSIC
utterances.text: I don't know which institute was involved. Mr. Sainovic knows that. But he told me that we need to secure sodium hydroxide or as it is also known caustic soda and to use mechanical resources to pull down those fibres to the ground, sprinkle them, and let them burn out.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So you addressed yourself to Mr. Sainovic?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOTA COSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You gave him the samples?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOTA COSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And then, after that he informed you as he did?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOTA COSIC
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You don't know which institute was involved?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOTA COSIC
utterances.text: I wasn't even interested in which institute was going to do it. What mattered to me was that I had a practical solution to deal with the problems I faced because the fibres were not my only problem. I had 30 per cent of all transformer stations destroyed in Nis, Bor, Novi Sad, all of them 400 kilo volts and I had to restore the supply of power in hydro-power stations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So, Mr. Cosic, if you could just complete this for me by going back to paragraph 17, which I know is about a separate matter but could you have it in front of you again. And in it you say that you and Mr. Sainovic agreed to approach the institute for nuclear and other raw materials and ask them for a solution. Now, did you approach that institute in connection with the hydrochloric acid?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that as far as hydrochloric acid is concerned, he approached that institute but I don't know that, he knows. All I know is that one of the institutes made a proposal, presented it to the government for review. They wanted approval for the government to purchase certain materials so that we could destroy this acid, and that job took a long time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Would you look at your tab number 5, that's the letter from Mr. Milosevic regarding the referendum. The translation of that document is 1D18, e-court page 348. You said that you had no occasion to see this letter, but the prime minister informed you about it and the government agreed and proclaimed a referendum, which was indeed held. You recall that?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOTA COSIC
utterances.text: Yes, I recall that. The government agreed and sent it to the Assembly of the Republic of Serbia for adoption. The government itself cannot proclaim a referendum, only the Assembly can do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember when that referendum took place and do you recall whether this issue contained in the invitation of the SFRY President Milosevic was indeed the issue for the referendum?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOTA COSIC
utterances.text: Yes, that was the question asked at the referendum and you know how the citizens responded.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Just tell us what you know. How did the citizens respond?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOTA COSIC
utterances.text: The citizens did not accept the participation of foreign factors in the resolution of Kosovo and Metohija problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember how many citizens turned out?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOTA COSIC
utterances.text: It's been such a long time. I couldn't possibly answer that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Just one more question. In paragraph 43 of your statement, you were shown document 1D084 dealing with the decisions of the government from 17th of June concerning humanitarian issues in Kosovo and Metohija. You said that you recalled the contents of these documents, you had dealt with them, and you were involved in the plan to implement this efficiently. Do you know whether this plan was indeed implemented and whether the citizenry in Kosovo was helped with supplies of food, construction material, and such-like?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOTA COSIC
utterances.text: Of course, I remember that. The plan was implemented. Minister Adrijan Milosavljevic and minister for construction and Mr. Milosavljevic was sent there to deal with the issue with local authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And was the government informed of the progress?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOTA COSIC
utterances.text: Of course it had to be informed because they supplied the resources and funding.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember whether the government was satisfied with the way that humanitarian aid was distributed and with the results achieved under that plan?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOTA COSIC
utterances.text: I don't recall that anybody had any objections or complaints at sessions of the government. We were happy that people living in Kosovo and Metohija were being supplied with the necessities.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Cosic, I have a few questions for you. There's no need for me to introduce myself because we know each other. May I -- in fact, you said in your statement that Vinca was 15 kilometres away?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOTA COSIC
utterances.text: I don't know the exact distance, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What I want to ask is: How far is Baric from Belgrade and does the town of Obrenovac lie between Baric and Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOTA COSIC
utterances.text: It's a difficult question. I believe that Baric is also 15 kilometres away and there's perhaps 6 or 7 kilometres between Baric and Belgrade -- Baric and Obrenovac, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And the same is the distance between Obrenovac and Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOTA COSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You said there was a danger of NATO air-strikes hitting Baric. You emphasised that you relocated material from many other hazardous installations, that's paragraph 1 of your statement -- sorry, 21 of your statement, and you enumerated these installations and factories.

utterances.speaker: ZIVOTA COSIC
utterances.text: Well, none of these factories were relocated before that because we had not been prepared for the relocation. NATO pre-empted us and they bombed Krusik in Valjevo, Sloboda in Cacak, the sodium factory in Pancevo, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What I'm trying to establish is that there was a real danger of hitting Baric?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOTA COSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: In paragraph 1, you said you were given an assignment from Prime Minister Marjanovic to organise the relocation of these materials and that there was a meeting on the 23rd of March.

utterances.speaker: ZIVOTA COSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: But you didn't say where the meeting was held?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOTA COSIC
utterances.text: In the building of the Republic of Serbia. I have to tell you that we held all the meetings there until the day when the General Staff building and even the building of the Republic of Serbia's government were bombed in Belgrade. After that, Prime Minister Marjanovic gave orders to relocate the seat of the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: In paragraph 16 you say: "I approached Deputy Federal Prime Minister Nikola Sainovic ..." Why him?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOTA COSIC
utterances.text: I approached him because he was my predecessor in the Ministry of Industry and Energy. He was the federal minister for economy and prime minister, and before all this he had worked at the smelting combine in Bor.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: He was also an experienced engineer?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOTA COSIC
utterances.text: Certainly, and I believe he spent his entire career working in industry. I was interested in people who knew their job.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So it was your decision?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOTA COSIC
utterances.text: It was my decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: When was that meeting held in the building of Jugometal? That's paragraph 17.

utterances.speaker: ZIVOTA COSIC
utterances.text: You see, we got that assignment on the 23rd of March. I got into my car the next day, went to Iskra factory in Baric, and I must say they gave me the runaround for all of 15 days. All this time I kept Nikola informed of what was going on and Nikola said, Let's first find a solution how to destroy these substances, and hopefully, in the meantime we'll find the cisterns to relocate. I'll talk to the institute, ask them to find a solution, to propose that solution to the government, the Government of Serbia must approve that solution because they needed the funding to purchase the appropriate materials. We had meetings every two or three days on this issue and I had to say that it was very time-consuming. We only managed to find a solution to relocate this acid outside of the perimeter in the second half of April, and when we removed the acid, we had frequent meetings later in the foreign ministry building with the Deputy Prime Minister Tomic.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So that meeting in Jugometal that you mentioned in paragraph 17 is about 15 days after the 23rd of March, when you were appointed?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOTA COSIC
utterances.text: Yes, 12, 15, 10, it's hard to say that now, but 10 days passed at least before we met again because he had his assignments and I had mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Why did you meet at Jugometal, was that a seat?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOTA COSIC
utterances.text: That was the headquarters of a foreign trade company, trading in metals, and we met there because Mr. Nikola Sainovic moved the federal government there. That's why he was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: When you got there was that a normal office or was it some sort of headquarters?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOTA COSIC
utterances.text: It was an office that Jugometal was using for its civilian needs.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers please slow down and pause between answer and question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Once he completed his military term of duty, he became a lieutenant or something. This is the first time that I'm hearing about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, you must ask that last question again because the interpreter was unable to keep up and translate it.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You gave us an answer that you never heard that he commanded anybody and I asked you whether --

utterances.speaker: ZIVOTA COSIC
utterances.text: I responsibly claim that I never heard that he was in any kind of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And you never saw?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOTA COSIC
utterances.text: No, no, no. He always sat by himself and was in civilian clothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. And during April and May you met several times with him?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOTA COSIC
utterances.text: Several times, more or less every two or three days.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And you would always -- when I finish my question, please, you can wait and when the text is fully typed out, perhaps then you can begin your answer. That would be the best way to do it. So in May of -- and April of 1999 you would meet with Sainovic and others every day, people who were dealing with the relocation, and you would discuss the course of that and the difficulties for this relocation?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOTA COSIC
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And all of those meetings took place in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOTA COSIC
utterances.text: All the meetings took place in Belgrade because we didn't have any other premises.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And how long did they last, these meetings?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOTA COSIC
utterances.text: Depends on the subject that was discussed. Sometimes it would be a good two hours long.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Now I would just like to ask you to tell me since when do you know Sainovic?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOTA COSIC
utterances.text: I've known Sainovic since the time he was energy minister in the government of Radovan Bozovic, he was my guest in Krusik. We talked then about economic topics. The entire government of the Republic of Serbia came because Krusik or Valjevo was an important partner to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: When you say you saw each other, you are also talking about conversations about the current situation?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOTA COSIC
utterances.text: Yes, that was part of his duties as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I was simply asking Mr. Fila also to observe the pause. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I would now like to ask you to briefly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I would certainly need more information on when they first met. You say that you knew Mr. Sainovic since he was energy minister in the Government of Radovan Bozic, so when was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think this was either in 1990 or 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: ZIVOTA COSIC
utterances.text: Possible. I don't really know.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And this Radovan he's Bozic or Bozovic?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOTA COSIC
utterances.text: Radovan Bozovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: For the transcript. Now I would like to ask you about something characteristic. Could you please give us a characteristic about Sainovic as a tradesman, as a political official when you met him. What were his characteristics?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOTA COSIC
utterances.text: I can say that as a person he's a great person, of a high education, that he's a good householder, takes good care of his family. He was a great businessman, and as for the kind of politician he was, I wasn't in the main or the Executive Board, so it's something that I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: All right. Very well. Thank you. That is all.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Just very briefly, Your Honours, I omitted to ask that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I omitted to ask that Mr. Cosic's statement and supplemental information be admitted into evidence. Sorry for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I see no objection to that, so --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- that will form part of the record. I see no other Defence counsel anxious to cross-examine, so over to you, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. Cosic, I just have a few questions for you. You said in your statement at paragraph 8 that you were under, in your view, no obligation, neither did you have any responsibility towards the president of Serbia, and you also said today that you were not duty-bound to send him documents about the work that you were doing.

utterances.speaker: ZIVOTA COSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Neither were either fellow ministers of the government, I take it in your view, duty-bound to send him information about the work they were doing?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOTA COSIC
utterances.text: No. They could send him information in writing with the agreement of the late Prime Minister Mirko Marjanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Is it that you are saying that it was a prime minister who had the responsibility, if any, to send him reports and to send him information; the ministers could not do so directly?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOTA COSIC
utterances.text: The ministers were not able to do that directly, but it was definite that the prime minister and the president were on the same line.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Are you aware that the Serbian Law on Government - and this for the record is P1862 - provide in Article 19 that at the request of the president the government "shall take a position on certain issues within its jurisdiction and inform the president thereof within a time he determines being not less than 48 hours." Are you aware that the Serbian Law on Government provides that the government shall - and I stress shall - inform the president?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOTA COSIC
utterances.text: I wasn't a prime minister of the Republic of Serbia, so I didn't deal with those matters. I was dealing with my own ministry and taking care of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, but in paragraph 8 of your statement you refer to the constitution and the organisation, the legal organisation of the powers of the government. All I'm asking you is whether or not you are or you were aware that the law provided that the government shall inform the president within 48 hours if he requested that?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOTA COSIC
utterances.text: I really don't know that because I wasn't dealing with those matters. Probably if that's what the law says, then that's how it was, but I really don't have that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In any case, your understanding was that the president was informed about the work of the government through the prime minister?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOTA COSIC
utterances.text: He should have been informed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said that President Milutinovic was interested in certain issues and you kept him informed. How did he communicate to the government his interest in certain issues? Did he make written requests?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOTA COSIC
utterances.text: I don't know why he was interested, but if he was interested in something he would probably address Prime Minister Mirko Markovic [as interpreted] directly in writing. I wasn't really interested in that, but as a friend of mine, person who he respected and took his opinions into account, he would call me, he would ask me specific questions what I thought about it, how to solve a specific problem, what he can tell the citizens who were calling him on a daily basis, will there be enough water, electricity, public transportation, all those matters that were important in the life of a city such as Belgrade. And, of course, I would go to him at his invitation. I thought that that was my civic and normal duty. I also said that according to the law, I was not obliged to inform him. My obligations ran to the prime minister of the government and the president of the Republic of Serbia. So these were moral obligations, civic obligations.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. To get back to my question which is about how he asked for information from the government. You said that he would probably address Prime Minister Markovic [sic] directly in writing. What I want to ask you: Do you know that he did in fact address Prime Minister Markovic directly in writing?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOTA COSIC
utterances.text: I was not chef de cabinet of President Mirko Marjanovic to receive his mail and to pass it on to someone else. I was a minister. I don't know what their communication was. I'm talking about the communication between myself as a minister of mining and energy and my human civic obligation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm asking you these questions because you told us that the information transmitted to the president from the government was through the prime minister. So all I'm asking is: What means did the president use to ask the prime minister for information from the government?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I believe the witness has answered that question already.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It seems --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In my submission --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It seems to have been answered, Mr. Stamp, is it not?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: My submission would be that he has not given a clear answer and he ought to be given an opportunity to give a clear answer. If he doesn't know how but he assumes it was in writing that is possibly an answer, but he said it was probably directly in writing. I want to know if he knows that as a fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think you've got the answer that he doesn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. I will note his answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Let's move on. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you know whether or not President Milutinovic contacted at any time the minister of interior directly for information about the work in the Ministry of Interior?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOTA COSIC
utterances.text: I don't have that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: From your answer I take it that you cannot say that Mr. Milutinovic would receive information about the work of the government only from the prime minister. It is possible that he could and did contact the minister of interior directly?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I think this is a construction which doesn't have any basis in the answer of the witness. The witness says: "I don't have that information." That is the only thing he said on the question of whether the minister of interior has sent anything to President Milutinovic. So he doesn't know about it. I don't know where it comes from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That seems right again, Mr. Stamp, does it not? Your question was: "Do you know whether or not President Milutinovic contacted at any time the minister of interior directly for information ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And he says: "I don't have that information."

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Earlier he had said that all the ministers only communicated with the president through the prime minister.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So if he does not have this information I'm just asking him to see it follows that he does not know whether or not all the ministers communicated with the president only through the prime minister.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I think you can take it that that must be the position in light of the answers he's giving. It's stating the obvious.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We know from the evidence of the last witness that the president can approach a minister directly and specifically ask for information from the minister, not just the provision you refer to about the government but there is one about approaching a minister direct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Indeed. But I -- notwithstanding that, the witness does -- has given evidence and has given a statement in which he says certain things about the limitations on the communication between the ministers and the president, and I thought I was entitled to ask him about his knowledge of that. Whether or not there's evidence before the Court from another witness because it might well go to what he knows and to his reliability if he's making statements without a sound basis in fact to make those statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: These are matters for debate later. Let's continue with the rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said that the work group involved in disposing of the hazardous material sent daily reports to Mr. Milutinovic because of the high human risk factor. Were those reports sent directly to the president by the work group?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOTA COSIC
utterances.text: No. They didn't have the right to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: They were sent through the -- through whom, may I ask?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOTA COSIC
utterances.text: The reports could have been sent only with the agreement of the Prime Minister Mirko Marjanovic to the Deputy Prime Minister Dragomir Tomic, and then he could be authorised to pass them on. But the prime minister had to be informed about each of those documents. I don't have any other information. I know about my ministry and that I could not do anything without the knowledge and permission of my prime minister. If the prime minister did agree, then the minister could send a letter to the president of the republic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, which paragraph was that, the quotation you took?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That's paragraph 19, a paraphrase of the sense of the paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: How did you know, Mr. Cosic, that the reports were sent to President Milutinovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I knew from the Deputy Prime Minister Dragomir Tomic about what our tasks were and anything that had to do with the economic department of the Government of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'll ask you the question again then. How did you know, Mr. Cosic, that the reports were sent to the president?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I had daily contacts with the Deputy Prime Minister Dragomir Tomic, and he showed me what the working group did out in the field and with the agreement of the prime minister. He passed that on to the president of the republic for his information, these reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So he told you that he sent daily reports to President Milutinovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's very easy when you just answer the questions directly, Mr. Cosic. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'm wondering if it is an appropriate time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It is indeed. We'll need to break at this stage for lunch. Mr. Cosic, please go with the usher, he will show you where you can wait until we resume, which will be at 1.45. Meanwhile, please do not discuss any aspect of the evidence in this case with anyone while you're outwith the courtroom. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.46 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You also referred to reports that were sent by the minister of interior to the president and you refer in your statement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember the reference to the minister of the interior in the statement of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. I think at paragraph 38 of his statement he referred to D -- 1D705 and 1D717. I don't know if I need to open them in e-court, but these are reports by the minister of interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, but these are reports from the minister of interior, but he doesn't say that these reports are the reports which were sent to president. And that was -- the question was aimed at to the president you refer in your statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Stamp, all the statement says is that he has been shown these documents and he doesn't recall them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And he refers to these documents in his statement. These documents, if we should open them, are reports of the minister of interior addressed to the president of the republic. He says, though he has not seen them, he presumes with a great degree of certainty that these are documents --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I withdraw my objection. The document 1D705 is, in fact, addressed to the president, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. Continue, Mr. Stamp, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, you don't remember, according to your statement, the particular documents that the minister of interior addressed to the president but you could speak about them with a greater degree of certainty according to you. Do you know how often the minister of interior sent reports of this nature to the president?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOTA COSIC
utterances.text: Is that a question for me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have that information. I really don't know. I don't have those -- that information, believe me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: How often in April and May - and I'm turning to something else now - how often in April and May did you meet with Mr. Sainovic and that's in 1999?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOTA COSIC
utterances.text: I didn't count how many times, but I know that every three or four days we were in touch. I would usually from my office, which was in the Srpski Ladara Street, it was the Jugopetrol building, walked to the office of Mr. Sainovic where we would discuss the matters that were mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you know whether or not he went to Kosovo from time to time in that period?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOTA COSIC
utterances.text: I don't have the information. He wasn't a member of the Serbian government for me to know where he went. I really don't have that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you know precisely what his role in Kosovo was, if any?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOTA COSIC
utterances.text: Believe me, I don't know. I told you he wasn't a member of the republican government; he was in the federal government. And I don't know what his duties were in relation to Kosovo and Metohija, if he had any duties at all. The best thing would be to ask somebody from the federal government. I was from the republican government. I know what the republican government did and I can have a quality dialogue on that here today.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: How many times did you meet with President Milosevic during the period 24 May 1999 to 10 June 1999?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOTA COSIC
utterances.text: I never Mr. Milosevic at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm so sorry, I meant President Milutinovic, I beg your pardon. How many times did you meet him in that period?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOTA COSIC
utterances.text: It's in the material here exactly when we had the joint meetings. He called me also several times for me to call back and to submit a report to him about the electricity supply, what the situation was with drinking water, will the hospitals have electricity, would we have enough fuels to heat the town. It was cold that April - and other matters like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, your statement does refer to at least one meeting with him during the period that I asked you about, but I just want to know if there were more than one meeting. How many meetings did you have with him in that period?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOTA COSIC
utterances.text: It's written here that we had a meeting on the 7th of April. If you look through the material, it says on the 24th of May. As for the other meeting -- other contacts, these were just telephone consultations between us. I didn't really keep a record how many times and what, but he would call me often. He was concerned. I could see that he was worried about the population, both of Belgrade and the population of the Republic of Serbia. He was the president of all the citizens who lived in the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So I take it then that you met him twice in that period?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOTA COSIC
utterances.text: We definitely met more than twice, but I noted down these two dates in my diary, dates for the meeting. As for the other contacts, I didn't keep a record. There was no need to do that. This is something that is easy, and I didn't need to write it down. Whatever he conveyed to me, I would go and do it. One of the tasks given to me by Mr. Milutinovic was to find a solution to develop a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cosic, just try to answer the question. Tell us roughly how often you met him.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Several times, but I cannot tell you whether it was three, four, five times. It was on a number of occasions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- and he would call me very often.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Following up on what you're saying, you're saying that one of the tasks given to you by Mr. Milutinovic was to find a solution to develop what?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOTA COSIC
utterances.text: A solution how to protect the citizens with low income from very expensive electricity. We introduced three different zones. Those who were using less were supposed to pay more and those who were using more were to pay -- those who were using less were to pay less and those who were using more electricity were to pay a higher rate. That was the problem we were dealing with.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And did he communicate this to you in the phone calls or when you met him personally or in writing?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOTA COSIC
utterances.text: Personally. We met in person, and he gave me this task orally.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I believe there is an omission in the transcript where on page 80, 20, I think the witness has said "that was the idea of Mr. Milutinovic and we implemented it." Maybe Mr. Stamp can -- I heard it in Serbian, that's for sure, but it is not in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You've heard that, Mr. Cosic. Can you tell us what it was you said after you told us that those who were using less electricity should pay less and those who were using more should pay more.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And you added something about that was the problem or that was the idea -- what was it you said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was the idea, the idea the president, Mr. Milutinovic, to protect citizens with low earnings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- and that those who had a lower standard of living so that we would be able to help them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The Government of Serbia you said met every seven days. When you say the Government of Serbia, do you mean the cabinet of the prime minister of Serbia? Is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOTA COSIC
utterances.text: The cabinet of the prime minister Mirko Marjanovic and the cabinet comprised his ministers, the ministers in the Government of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And you also indicated that you were present at a meeting of a government when Mr. Milutinovic attended in respect to the Holbrooke-Milosevic Agreement.

utterances.speaker: ZIVOTA COSIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: At the time when Mr. Milutinovic attended that meeting of the government, was the government composed of one party or was it a type of coalition?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOTA COSIC
utterances.text: It was a coalition government, in coalition with the Serbian Radical Party.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Who -- well, how many times do you know of Mr. Milutinovic attending meetings of the government?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOTA COSIC
utterances.text: He rarely attended the government meetings. He would attend only when he believed it was important in order for the cabinet of Mirko Marjanovic to function well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And this would be approximately how many times in your experience?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOTA COSIC
utterances.text: You're asking me as if I was counting.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That's why I said approximately.

utterances.speaker: ZIVOTA COSIC
utterances.text: Perhaps a couple of times when some very important questions were being decided on, questions that were important for the functioning of the Government of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you remember some of those questions, give us some examples of those questions?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOTA COSIC
utterances.text: There is information here, let me just find it, when he was at a meeting of the republican government, in relation to issues pertaining to Kosovo and Metohija. This is the 13th of October, 1998, when the government issued a statement dealing with all the questions of vital interest for the citizens of Kosovo and Metohija with deadlines built in, with deadlines given for what had to be done by when. And, as far as I know, all that was agreed on was actually carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Is that the meeting in respect to the Milosevic-Holbrooke Agreement you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOTA COSIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Apart from that which is in your statements, what other questions that were important to the functioning of the Government of Serbia did Mr. Milutinovic attend government meetings in regard to, if you can remember?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOTA COSIC
utterances.text: One of the questions that Mr. Milutinovic was interested in was if we had an adequate supply of fuels, because when the NATO aggression on our country started in March, when preparations were underway for the spring sowing. And you know for many years we were under sanctions, so we lacked a lot of energy sources. So the little we had would be redirected to the sowing works. If we didn't sow enough grains and vegetables, we would not be able to feed the citizens of Serbia. So at that time it was an important question, but Mr. Milutinovic did not attend that particular meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Cosic, you are an intelligent man. You are being asked at this moment about matters that were on the agenda when Mr. Milutinovic attended cabinet meetings, not when he did not attend. So would you please answer that question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that he would come to government meetings to express an interest in those matters as well. You asked me how many times he came. I said he came several times.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We've moved --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- put this question at the very beginning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We have moved on from that to ask you for examples of the matters which would be on the agenda when he attended.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that he was once at a government meeting when the agricultural issues were being dealt with. I remember that. I wasn't constantly attending government meetings either because I had a thousand and one problems at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- I had to resolve matters relating to the functioning of the electrical energy industry. I had to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cosic --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- make the oil refineries work as well at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- please just concentrate on the questions. We have enough to take in from the answers to the questions without also having to hear every additional thing you think we ought to be told. It's a matter for counsel to ask you questions. It may be a translation problem, but after telling us about the agricultural issue you then told us that Mr. Milutinovic did not actually attend that meeting. Now, have you been wrongly interpreted by the interpreters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't understand. I said that he would come or he came to a government meeting to get acquainted or to find out about those matters. I said that and you said how many times did he come and I said he came several times. But I remember once when he was present agricultural issues were discussed, but I didn't attend all the government meetings because I had duties in relation to the electrical supply industry, the oil refining industry, and so on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't need to know what may have been distracting you. But your answer was: "One of the questions Mr. Milutinovic was interested in is we had an adequate supply of fuels" and you went on to tell us that it was important to direct these -- possibly you said to the sowing works, which I assume is farms. "If we didn't sow enough grains and vegetables, we would not be able to feed the citizens of Serbia" --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just a moment, just listen to all I've got to say. At that time it was an important question, but Mr. Milutinovic did not actually attend that particular meeting. Now, is that a mistranslation of what you said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't say anything wrong. Who said that he didn't attend? I said that he was present at a government meeting when this was exactly, I don't know, but I know that it was in the month of March.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Does the interpreter have any way of assisting us on this? We're talking about lines 19 to 21 of page 83.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter heard him say that Mr. Milutinovic did not attend that meeting, but we could be wrong. I think the witness is the only person who could clarify that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, possibly it can be reviewed by listening to the tape. So that should be done and we should be given a report of what was actually said so that this part of the transcript can be clarified. Are there any other examples you can give us of occasions when Mr. Milutinovic attended a cabinet meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am not able to do that because I was burdened with my own problems so I really don't know whether there was any other occasion that he attended. Probably other witnesses who come to testify knows that, too. I mean, they were also members of the republican government. I just didn't expect something like this to happen, so I didn't really keep a record. It was a long time ago. 1999 was a long time ago and time has taken its toll on my memory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said that he attended meetings where issues that were important to the function of the government of Serbia were being dealt with and I think somewhere else you said he did so to express his position on these issues and also to get acquainted and to find out what is happening in respect to these issues. Can you describe further what role he played at these meetings that he attended?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOTA COSIC
utterances.text: Ministers have a role to play, not the president of the republic. He only came to get informed, to have a clear insight into the work of the Government of the Republic of Serbia, and that in contacts with the citizens of Serbia, he could have his own position on these particular questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, you did say that he expressed himself on these issues, he expressed his position on these issues. Are you saying that he did not express his position on these important issues when he attended the government meetings? Are you changing what you said earlier?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOTA COSIC
utterances.text: I said that the Government of the Republic of Serbia took a position on all questions which were on the agenda of the republican government, and the ministers would vote. He can be there as a guest to get acquainted with the matters, but he does not have a right to vote. He can make suggestions, but if -- as to whether the government would accept that or not, that is another matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When he attended meetings of the government, who initiated or who made arrangements for his presence there? Do you know how that was arranged?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOTA COSIC
utterances.text: I don't know how it was arranged, but it could not be resolved without going through Prime Minister Mirko Marjanovic. He held everything in his hands. We were acting as a solid team under his guidance.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you know of any meeting that he attended that dealt with the complaints of crimes being committed against the Kosovar Albanian population by Serbian police?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOTA COSIC
utterances.text: I don't have that information, and as far as I know, this was not brought before the Government of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cosic, you told us that the prime minister was ill in September 1998. Who carried --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, I didn't say that. I never said that the prime minister was sick in September. When I said that today, I said that about Andro Milosavljevic that he got sick in September 1998, but I did not say that about Prime Minister Mirko Marjanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, it must be my mistake. So the prime minister continued to preside over meetings of the government until June 1999?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] President -- Prime Minister Mirko Marjanovic was not prime minister until June, but he was the prime minister until October 2000 when the elections were set.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't understand that answer. He was not prime minister until June 1999?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not only until June 1999, but after June 1999 as well. We didn't have a different prime minister.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that. My question is: Did he actually preside over meetings of the government until June 1999?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I know, yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Did he preside at every meeting you attended?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's a difficult question. I really don't remember. What I know is that whenever I attended government meetings, Prime Minister Mirko Marjanovic was there. But I said that I wasn't at every government meeting because he had entrusted me with resolving other issues that needed to be resolved as needed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I asked a one-line --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, I asked a one-line question there. Was it difficult to translate that into Serbian?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm listening to Your Honours in English, so I don't know if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: -- what was the translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's just that you ask a simple question and you get an answer that doesn't address the question, and you then have to wonder is that translation or is it the witness who has a difficulty. And I wonder if anyone heard that question can tell me if it was a question that was easily translated into Serbian or not. Mr. Fila, can you help?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What the matter is you asked him whether Prime Minister Marjanovic was a president until June and what happened is that he thought -- whether he was the prime minister up until June, but he was the prime minister later as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I follow that. That's not the question I'm concerned about. If you see the next question which was: "Did he preside at every meeting you attended?" Now, is that easily translated into Serbian?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It has been excellently translated. It's not a problem sentence to translate at all, but the witness responded in a complicated manner.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that whenever I attended a government meeting, it was chaired by Mirko Marjanovic. I don't know if somebody else substituted for him whenever I did not attend government meeting. That I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis -- sorry, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Turning to the meeting that you referred to specifically in your statement, that is a meeting in respect to the Holbrooke-Milosevic Agreement, was there dissent in the government about whether or not to accept the terms of that agreement?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOTA COSIC
utterances.text: I don't have that information. From what I know, the government's position on that was unanimous.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. Before the government took a unanimous position on it, there were discussions in the cabinet in respect to it that Mr. Milutinovic attended - I see that from your statement - that's correct?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOTA COSIC
utterances.text: Please tell me the number of the statement where you saw this -- I mean the paragraph number in the statement.

utterances.speaker: ZIVOTA COSIC
utterances.text: I don't know what kind of translation you have, but here it says that President Milosevic informed the government of the Milosevic-Holbrooke Agreement. There was no disagreement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This is an important -- just hold on. There is an important apparent mistake in that transcript because what I'm reading says President Milutinovic. Is this wrong, should it be President Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: It was Milutinovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Sorry. Please continue. We're --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What I want to know is this: I take it that if he merely -- that if President Milutinovic was merely interested in informing the cabinet about the agreement, he could have sent a copy to the cabinet. He would not have needed to attend it personally. What I'd like to know is: Did Mr. Milutinovic at that cabinet meeting advocate a position in respect to the government accepting that agreement?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOTA COSIC
utterances.text: I don't remember what he advocated, but I do remember the position taken by the government on the issue. It's been a long time since that cabinet session to today, so all I can tell you is what the cabinet decided. And what other people said in their discussion, I really can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
