utterances.text: Can I ask you this, and I'm moving on, and it's just to get your assessment of the practical realities of government at the time. You say that President Milutinovic was interested in a variety of matters, and as a result, reports were sent to him. And you yourself reported to him quite frequently.

utterances.speaker: ZIVOTA COSIC
utterances.text: Orally, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes. Should a member of the government neglect to do important tasks and fail to report to Mr. Milutinovic about it, do you -- what could he have done? Let me give you an example. If you had not removed the ammonia from the plant that was so close to Belgrade --

utterances.speaker: ZIVOTA COSIC
utterances.text: The acid?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The acid, and you failed to explain that to Mr. Milutinovic or informing about -- inform him about it, what could he do in respect to such a dangerous situation? What could he do as president?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOTA COSIC
utterances.text: The president could ask Mirko Marjanovic to dismiss me as prime minister -- I mean he could ask the prime minister to dismiss me. That might have been one measure. That job had to be completed by me or by someone else. As it was I who was given the task, I took it seriously and I performed it conscientiously. But I really cannot imagine anyone who had received such a task, refusing to complete it, and thus getting in a situation where he might be dismissed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Moving on. You said that the government was unprepared, as far as you know, and nobody really believed that NATO would attack. Do you know about the levels of military preparation that had taken place in Kosovo on March 2 -- by March 24, 1999?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOTA COSIC
utterances.text: I can't answer that question because the cabinet of the Republic of Serbia did not have the army in its sphere of competence. That was at the federal level, so I couldn't answer that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, do you know of the police in Kosovo making any steps in preparation for a possible attack?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOTA COSIC
utterances.text: I really don't have that information. I spent a lot of time in Kosovo and Metohija, starting in 1980 as a businessman, and later on, I had been there and there were different problems, various problems, kidnappings of workers and so on. But I don't believe --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cosic, please confine yourself to the question you're asked which is about the 24th of March, 1999. What preparations had been made by the MUP at that stage to account for the possibility of an attack by NATO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have that information. That subject matter was not -- I don't have that information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are you saying on full responsibility that the government were not discussing the activities of the MUP just about the time of the NATO bombing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have that information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you either -- you know the answer yes or no because you were a member of the government, attending government meetings.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not attend each and every cabinet session. As I said, the ones I attended, I say, did not have that on the agenda.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So at -- you say on full responsibility that at no meeting you attended were the preparations that the MUP might be making for the possibility of a NATO attack ever discussed. Is that your position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's my position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So we have to have a picture of a Republic of Serbia government that never discussed, as far as you were aware, the question of what special arrangements might be appropriate for the MUP just in case NATO arrived?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I assert with full responsibility that it was not. We didn't want to move out of the government building of the Republic of Serbia because we did not believe there would be air-strikes. It had to be struck first for us to move out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you know that that's quite a different question from the one I'm asking, but we'll now move on. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. Cosic, do you know anything about an offensive by the MUP in March 1998?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have to object here. I would like the reference from the transcript or the statement where does -- where does this cross comes from, because I don't remember that this gentleman discussed MUP, its actions, meetings. If it's in the direct examination, I would like to have the reference please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, there must be a misunderstanding here. Cross-examination is not confined to matters which arise in examination-in-chief. He's perfectly entitled to ask a much wider range of questions in cross-examination. So that can't be a basis for your objection, Mr. Lukic. If you have another one, please state it; but in the absence of another one, I will repel that will objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you know of reports about an assault by MUP forces in March 1998 at Donji Prekaz, where reportedly 54 Kosovo Albanians were killed?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOTA COSIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you know about reports of similar offensives around the middle of 1998, July 1998, where the entire civilian population or most of the civilian population of Orahovac-Malisevo had to leave their homes? Do you know about that or reports of that about that?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOTA COSIC
utterances.text: If I had heard anything about it, I would not have allowed myself in June 1998 to hold a meeting in Kosovo and Kosovo B thermo-electric power-plants with the leadership. I would certainly not have gone to Feronikel Glogovac to attend the meetings of the management board which started at 2000 hours in the evening, have dinner in Pristina and then go to Belgrade by night. I really did not have such information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Again there may be a translation difficulty because the question was about the month of July and the answer is about June. So, Mr. Cosic, the question that you were asked was whether you knew of similar offensives around the middle of 1998, July 1998. Does that affect your answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said I did not have this information.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: This -- the two events I just referred to is from evidence we have heard before the Court, I just wanted to know if you heard reports about them. This is from evidence of John Crosland, a witness who testified here. He also said that he, himself, saw between 200 and 300 villages burnt throughout 1998 and into 1999. Did you hear reports of these -- of the destruction of these villages by Serbian forces at that time?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOTA COSIC
utterances.text: I did not have this information. I really haven't heard of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So where you claim that the position - and that is in paragraph 6 of your statement - the position and the policies adopted by the government and its prime minister were to resolve the situation in Kosovo and Metohija peacefully to ensure the security of all citizens, regardless of their ethnicity, you make that statement without any knowledge of reports of these events and without having attended meetings where MUP activities were discussed just at about the time of the conflict with NATO?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOTA COSIC
utterances.text: I assert with responsibility that the position and policy of the Government of the Republic of Serbia was that all outstanding issues should be resolved peacefully and through diplomatic means.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I have nothing further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Cosic, just a few questions regarding your response on pages 82 and 83 up to line 14. Mr. Cosic, in your statement you told us in para 8, you said that as the minister -- as a minister in the Government of Serbia you had no responsibility and no obligation towards the president of the Republic of Serbia and that you were only accountable to the prime minister who gave you assignments, as did the Assembly of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOTA COSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Cosic, you were appointed by the Assembly of the Republic of Serbia, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOTA COSIC
utterances.text: I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: May I just say that, not that I want to object to every leading question, but we might now be entering a phase where I would ask, respectfully, that the questions be in non-leading form.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stamp. Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Cosic, from whom did you receive your assignments?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOTA COSIC
utterances.text: Prime Minister Mirko Marjanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Was he the only person giving you assignments that you were duty-bound to execute?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOTA COSIC
utterances.text: The only one.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Did the prime minister of Serbia, who issued you assignments, have sole authority to demand reports and progress reports from you?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The deputy prime minister Tomic could also have asked for reports because he was in charge of economy.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No damage has been done by that because the answer was different, but you can see that the form of the question would give rise to concern.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour. I'm very sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Cosic, who had the authority to require reports from you and to whom were you obliged to provide such reports?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOTA COSIC
utterances.text: I've already said, Prime Minister Marjanovic, but I could also report to Deputy Prime Minister Dragomir Tomic, save for materials that were reserved for the cabinet.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Did you have the obligation when you were performing a certain duty to send -- to present reports or maybe briefs to the president of the republic?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOTA COSIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Cosic, who had the authority to ask that you be recalled or replaced?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOTA COSIC
utterances.text: Very difficult question. I really don't know. Anybody could ask for it, but it's questionable whether the government would accept it and present it to the Assembly for review.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So was the prime minister able to ask for your replacement and of whom?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOTA COSIC
utterances.text: Yes, the prime minister was able to do that and he would have to ask the Assembly of Serbia, which appointed me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Was the prime minister the only one who had the authority to ask for your replacement?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOTA COSIC
utterances.text: Any proposal for recall or replacement had first to be presented to the prime minister and then the Assembly of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Just one more question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Just bear with me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No further questions for this witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, we have to deal with exhibits, I think. 1D746, 747, and 742, that's tab 10, 11, and 5 may not have been referred to in any of the evidence. 5 possibly is okay because of 1D18.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But the other two have they been referred to?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, no, Your Honours, they have been added to the list. We don't seek to introduce this as evidence. We were just notified by our colleagues from the Prosecution side in one of the Rule 68 disclosure that -- about these two documents, and we just asked the witness to -- if he recognised them and he didn't. So that is why they were not in his 92 ter statement nor in the supplement. We just included them in this list --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: For -- in case, in case the subject was brought up in the court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, they will not be admitted, that's 1D747 --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And 1D746 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- and 1D746. Unless any objection is taken by any party to the others which are mentioned in the statement but have not been explored, then these will be admitted as part of the evidence in the statement. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honours, we object only in respect to 1D82.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Which tab is that?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Tab 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, that's 1D706.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm not sure if it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's tab 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I believe this document --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: [Indiscernible]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: -- is admitted already and it's in the list that it was admitted on the 31st of March -- no, I'm sorry, let me just consult.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It has been confirmed to me that that has been admitted, so I have no objection to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So the --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It's a newspaper -- yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So all the documents referred to in the 92 ter statement which have not already been admitted or in respect of which we have not determined they will not be admitted will be admitted; and the same applies in respect of the exhibits in relation to the previous witness. I tried to make that clear at the end of his examination-in-chief when you told me that every one of the exhibits referred to in each of the paragraphs of his statement had either been admitted or were referred to in his statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cosic, that completes your evidence; thank you for coming to the Tribunal to give it. You may now leave the courtroom with the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we're just waiting for our case manager to distribute the binders for the next witness, Mr. Jovan Kojic. He should be here any minute now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That may give me a chance then to raise another matter with you. There was an order made on the 9th of August which required action by both you and the Prosecution to tidy up the situation in relation to the two constitutions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm aware of that order, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It really needs to be --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It really needs to be attended to before your case is concluded.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour. Well, we have sent our -- I have talked to Mr. Hannis, and we basically agree. And we have sent a draft motion to him for his approval.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Since I'm here in court, I don't know if that has happened --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In the mean time -- it will be filed today, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We would be grateful if you would deal with that today. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Just bear with us, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, we can invite the witness and our associate will help with the binders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. That's Jovan Kojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Just to save the time. Yes, Mr. Jovan Kojic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, can we have the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, just before -- before we start, we have amendment of notification for Witness Kojic. And as I suggested before Mr. Cosic entered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sorry?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's the supplemental information --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, for Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That is 1D754, and also in light of -- of the discussion yesterday, we have added 1D62 and 1D66, which we will be presenting to Mr. Kojic. And we notified the -- our colleagues from the Prosecution about our intention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And as far as we know, there was no objection from their part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you have any problem with that, Mr. Stamp?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Kojic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration to speak the truth by reading aloud the document which will now be placed before you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You will now be examined by Mr. Zecevic. Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Kojic.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN KOJIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kojic, just one caution because I know this is your first time appearing before this Tribunal. We need to make a brief pause between questions and answers for the benefit of the interpretation. It's important, because only in that way can we get both questions and answers properly on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN KOJIC
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kojic, would you please for the record give us your full name.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN KOJIC
utterances.text: My name is Jovan Kojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Occupation?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN KOJIC
utterances.text: Civil servant.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You gave us a statement on the 27th of July, 2007, including an annex which is a sketch made by you. And then you made a supplement to that statement on the 12th of August this year. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN KOJIC
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: These are binders of documents related to your evidence. Would you please open binder 1. You can lower the second one for the time being. You see your statement in that binder 1 and your supplementary statement is in binder 2. Your statement is marked 1D741 and your supplementary statement is 1D754. Over the past few days you reviewed these two statements. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN KOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Since you reviewed them, can you confirm for us that the facts stated there truthfully reflect the events described by you to the best of your knowledge and recollection?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN KOJIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And if you were asked the same questions today, Mr. Kojic, you would give the same answers, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN KOJIC
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kojic. In the office, or rather, the office of the president of Serbia became your place of work when, do you remember the year or the date?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN KOJIC
utterances.text: 1st January 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned it in your statement but very briefly. How many personnel formed the inner core of the office of President Milutinovic?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN KOJIC
utterances.text: Five of us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In paragraph 2 of the statement, is 1977 a misprint for 1997?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Oh, yes, in -- I'm sorry, Your Honour, in the Serbian version it's 1997. So that's -- I wasn't really aware of what you were referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't think I've encountered so many translation or interpretation problems in one day as today.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, it's one of those days, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And we have three -- we are having this is our third witness, so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kojic, you have made a sketch on the last page of your statement, that page is marked annex 1 --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And I would ask if that can be produced either on the e-court. It's annex 1 of the 92 ter statement of Mr. Kojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On that sketch, we see what it looked like approximately. Do you have the sketch in front of you? It should also be on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Could the usher help.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The usher will show you how ...

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry? I'm sorry, there is some technical matter right now, Your Honour. Would the usher please explain to the witness how he can draw on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kojic, you can use this pen to make markings on the document and then the document can be saved if there's something you wish to mark on it. Mr. Kojic, you can touch the screen with that pen and -- do you understand?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN KOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Believe me, I'm very poor at technology myself. Mr. Kojic, this is a sketch you made, is it not?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN KOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. It's just a very rough sketch. I didn't actually expect it to be used.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Under 1 you indicated the room where President Milutinovic sat, his office in the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN KOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Could you please verify this again on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN KOJIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So what you have now marked in blue is the number 1, you've circled it, and this is the office where President Milutinovic sat, is it not?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN KOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Could you please indicate the desk at which you sat and circle it, please.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN KOJIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And mark it with an A.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN KOJIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So what is circled in office number 3, circled in blue and marked A, that is the desk at which you sat when you were in your usual place in the Presidency of Serbia. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN KOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can we have an IC number of this exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be IC135, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kojic, when you were in the spot you have just indicated, you were able to see all the persons entering President Milutinovic's office, were you not?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN KOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Also, very briefly, about the technology or the procedures employed in the office, you said there were three computers which were all linked up in a network. Can you explain very briefly how this functioned, how it was done technologically and how it operated, I mean.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN KOJIC
utterances.text: Well, the database was in the computer at which I sat. The other two computers, one was here and the other was here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Just a minute. If you're marking on the picture, please, could you mark it again with the pen, please. And, please, put B and C where the other two computers are.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN KOJIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So one computer marked B was in office number 2 and C was on the desk next to yours in office number 3. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN KOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kojic --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be IC136, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Any one entry into one of the computers could be seen on all the others. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN KOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Apart from this uniform database, you also had a telephone system for the use of the president's office. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN KOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And from that telephone system all conversations in the Presidency were conducted. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN KOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And calls were switched to President Milutinovic from that system or he would use that system to make phone calls with the assistance of someone from the office, one of you?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN KOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kojic, in paragraph 18 you -- of your statement you spoke about an incident in early 1998 on the occasion of the action to arrest Adem Jashari and his death. Do you remember that? That's what you wrote in paragraph 18.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN KOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I remember it well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Could you just explain very briefly where you saw this, what you saw, what the consequence was.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN KOJIC
utterances.text: That evening I was on duty in the office. It was 9.00 or 10.00 in the evening. I was watching the broadcast on Sky News. One evening -- one moment.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Footage of the police action in the Jashari Mahala was broadcast. I saw that this was quite a serious action involving an APC, armoured personnel carrier, and I felt that it was important for me to call the president and tell him that this was being broadcast on television, so that he too could watch if he felt it necessary. He could watch it on Sky News. On the next day, he said we should call Minister Stojiljkovic --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The minister of the interior?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN KOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, the minister of the interior, Stojiljkovic. And it was I who did that. The minister, however, did not respond. There was no reply even after several calls made by me. I spoke to his secretary more than once, and she always said either that he wasn't in or that he would call back as soon as he could. This went on for two or three days. He did not respond. The president asked what was going on. He was angry. He asked why there was no reply, and I tried to convey to him the explanation given by Minister Stojiljkovic's secretary. However, as the minister still did not respond, I remember the president saying we are now going to write a letter to the minister demanding that he explain what happened in Jashari Mahala. The letter was written, sent, and to the best of my knowledge no answer ever arrived. I remember it was quite brief but it contained a request that this event be explained.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kojic, how long after these fruitless attempts to make contact by telephone was this letter to Minister Stojiljkovic written?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN KOJIC
utterances.text: I can't be sure, but maybe two or three days.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kojic, you say there was never any response to that letter. How can you be sure that is the case?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN KOJIC
utterances.text: Well, I would have known because we employees in the office discussed this among ourselves, wondering how such a thing could happen, how it could come about that a letter from the president failed to elicit a response, how one could fail to respond to his phone calls. That had really never happened before.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, Mr. Kojic, when the mail arrived in the presidential building, how was it sorted? Could you explain this?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN KOJIC
utterances.text: The mail arrived in our office, and whatever was to be entered into the ledger was entered by us. We then put this in a plastic or paper cover, and then we put this in the president's inbox. Whatever was not within the sphere of work of the president was sent to the central clerk's office, where it was registered and then sent to the persons tasked with processing mail concerning various kinds of subjects, such as complaints, pardons, financial or organisational matters, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Just to clarify one thing. On page 111, these covers as you call them they were paper covers, were they not?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN KOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were greenish in colour. It -- these covers were formatted with numbers and ...

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 6 you explained that all the documents, press clippings, and so on were summarized in a brief information document for the president. Just explain how this was done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The translation is in paragraph 6, but that doesn't appear to be right. Which paragraph are you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, please. All the news, for instance, bulletins, briefs from the foreign office, news from the internet, agency news, all the important news that reached us for that day we summarized on one or two pages and we did this usually by quoting the key sentences on a series of topics. And we always sought to make it as concise and as clear as possible. That was the whole point, so that we wouldn't have to put before the president all these different papers from different sources. We summarized the whole material on a couple of pages or if certain statements were made concerning Yugoslavia by important international factors. We would quote them. That's about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That document was for the president's information, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN KOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you help me with one thing. How much coverage of the Jashari event was there in the media?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I think it was quite amply covered, especially by the foreign media; and about ours ... I cannot remember exactly how much coverage -- how much of that coverage reached the president.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And would all of that not be summarized by you or one of your associates and given to the president to make sure he was fully informed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we treated that piece of news like all the others. We put in an effort to provide all the statements made on account of that event and all the important news, and we treated it like all the other events.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So you recorded it, you got no report from the minister. What did the president do after that about what the foreign media were calling the disproportionate use of force by the police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I remember very clearly that he was angry because the minister was not responding and because he had not received a written report in response to his letter. As for the others, I couldn't tell.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So the president just left it at that, did he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't hear the witness's answer. Something was wrong with the microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Could you repeat your answer, please, the interpreter didn't hear it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wouldn't know about any further action, if any, that he took.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are you not being presented here, though, as a person who knew all the inner workings of the president's office?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I worked there and I can tell you about all that I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zecevic. Just one moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry about that. Please continue, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell me, please, Mr. Kojic, very briefly - and I believe we will have to come back to this issue tomorrow and I will then show you some documents - in para 29, you state that the president very rarely left the building to attend meetings. Could you explain very briefly what the protocol of Serbia meant and what it envisaged.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN KOJIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, anybody who met with the president came to the president's office. The president very rarely left the building of the Presidency, and he only went to the office of the president of Yugoslavia or the Supreme Defence Council, and those were the only occasions when he left his office.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In para 34 you say that the president's service and the president himself were involved in the political process of trying to resolve the problems of Kosovo and Metohija, and you also referred to the declaration of the 18th of March, his offer to be the guarantor of that process, the so-called three plus three talks, talks with Mr. Chris Hill and his associates. Mr. Kojic, you know all this from doing your job within the building of the Presidency? This is -- these are all things that you know first-hand?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN KOJIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 35 you said that at the request of the president you even assisted Professor Markovic and Professor Kutlesic regarding some documents. Would you tell us very briefly which documents.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN KOJIC
utterances.text: A draft agreement it was, the draft agreement discussed by Professor Markovic and Professor Kutlesic, with Christopher Hill, James O'Brien, and their associates and there were a number of versions of that draft agreement in Serbian, Serbo-Croat, and English.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I see the time and I think it's appropriate place for me to -- thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Kojic, that brings our court day to an end, I'm afraid. We're not in a position to continue though we would like to, so you have to return tomorrow, and that will be at 9.00 tomorrow morning. Meanwhile, overnight it's very important that you do not discuss your evidence, that's the evidence you have given or the evidence you may yet give with anyone at all. You can talk to whoever you like about whatever you like except about the evidence. So please leave the courtroom now with the usher and return here to recommence your evidence at 9.00 tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And we will adjourn now until 9.00 tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 16th day of August, 2007, at 9.00 a.m. 19 20 21 22 23 24

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 3.31 p.m.,
